messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slows a half-step before the yard proper and lets Bram take the lead on the track — the man in chain mail is the one a warden expects to talk to. He keeps his hands loose and off his sword, visibly empty.

While they walk in, he isn't looking at the warden. He's reading the yard: the sheds and their doors, the terraces above for anyone lying flat, the spoil heaps, the ground around the dropped tools — footprints, blood, dragged marks, anything that says *why* a quarry crew puts its hammers down and walks off mid-morning. And the house itself: shutters open or closed, how many sets of boots by the door.

Low, to the other two, not moving his lips much: "Place is empty and he's not surprised to see us. Bram, you talk. Sefa, stay near me. I'll watch the high ground."

Then he waits for the warden to speak first.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Tools left out, cart left loaded,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa. “Something stopped work in a hurry.”

I walk into the yard toward the house, shield on my arm but sword sheathed, watching the sheds and lower cut as I go. I stop a few paces from the man, leaving his doorway clear.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I glance back at the idle cart. “Everyone all right here?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa slows as the quarry comes into full view, her eyes moving over the scattered tools and the half-loaded cart before settling on the man in the doorway. She says quietly, to Pell and Bram, "No work being done, but someone waited for us to arrive. Keep it civil, not friendly."

She walks forward a few steps, well short of the doorway, raises an empty hand, and calls, "Well met. We're sent from the apothecary Maela Thorn in Beregost, out on her errand. Are you the warden of Whitestone?"

scenes.narration:
The yard is bigger up close than it looked from the bend. White dust lies over everything, fine as flour, and it holds a record of the last day for anyone who knows how to read one.

Pell reads it while Bram walks in front. The terraces above are bare. The faces are pale and stepped, there's no shadow deep enough for a man to lie flat in, and the only things moving up there are swallows working the cracks. The sheds stand shut. The two lower ones have their doors pulled to and barred from outside, which nobody does in a hurry. The tools by the lower cut weren't dropped. The hammers lie with their heads together, and the wedges are stacked in a little pile beside them, the way men set down tools they mean to leave. There's no blood anywhere and no drag marks in the dust. The traces on the half-loaded cart were unbuckled, not cut, and the straps hang neatly over the shaft. A broad churned band of bootprints runs from the yard down the cart track, a dozen men or more walking together and not running. It's a day old by the dust settled in the heel-marks, and the hoofprints of a single mule go along with them. The party's own fresh prints lie over all of it now.

The house has its front shutters open. One window at the side is closed. By the door there's one stool, one tin cup on the sill and one pair of boots, the ones on the man wearing them.

Bram stops a few paces short of the doorway and leaves the man room. Sefa stops farther back with her empty hand raised. The warden looks at the shield, then the sheathed sword, then Pell's loose hands, and last at Sefa. He takes his time about it.

"Hale," he says. "Osric Hale. I'm the warden."

He looks past Bram at the cart for a moment, as if it had asked the question.

"Nobody's hurt. They walked. Noon bell yesterday, the lot of them." He shifts his weight in the doorway but doesn't step out of it. "Thorn's case is inside. Sealed, like she wanted."

His keys clink once as his arms tighten across his apron.

"She pay for it? Because somebody's been paid for that salt. Three weeks I've had no wages from the Gate for my men, and no answer to my letters. The case stays where it is till I know whose pocket that money's sitting in."

Behind him, the thin grey smoke keeps rising from the chimney into a sky that's already white with heat.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I settle my shield at my side. “Three weeks unpaid is no small thing. But we’re hired carriers, Hale. Ninety gold between us on delivery, and nothing if we miss her buyer’s coach at sunset. I haven’t seen what she paid for the salt.”

I glance at the neatly stacked tools. “Your men left things in good order. I spoke too soon about trouble.”

Then I meet his eyes. “Who owes their wages, and who took payment for the case? If you’ve a bill or a letter tying the two together, let’s see it. What would satisfy you enough to let us carry it out today?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa says, low, to Bram: "He's not a bandit. He's a man holding the only thing he has left to bargain with."

Then, to Osric, with her hands still open and her voice steady: "No one's paid us to take that case against your will. We don't carry wages from the Gate, and we won't pretend to. But we'll be in Beregost by sunset, and we can put your question directly to Maela Thorn — whether she knows whose pocket that money's sitting in. That's more than three weeks of letters have got you." She pauses, watching his face rather than his keys. "A sealed case kept here past nightfall buys nobody's supper, Master Hale. Let it go with us, and let your question go with it."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't move his eyes from the yard while Hale talks. When the man finishes, he glances once at the two lower sheds — barred from outside — and then at the chimney, and only then at Hale.

Low, to Bram and Sefa, barely moving his mouth: "He's not holding the case against us. He's holding it against the Gate. We're just the nearest hands. And someone barred those two sheds from the outside before the crew left — you don't do that to keep tools in."

Then, a step behind Bram's shoulder, still not crowding the doorway, in an even, Lower City voice:

"Master Hale. We're hired carry, not her counting-house — she pays us on delivery, same as she's likely to pay you, which is why she's in a hurry and you're not. Nobody's sent us with your wages, and nobody's going to send them to a quarry that's gone quiet." A small nod toward the cart track. "Thorn's buyer leaves Beregost for the Gate at sunset. If you've got letters that want answering, that coach is the fastest road your complaint has had in three weeks. Write it, seal it, we carry it with the case and put it in her hand with the salt. You've got our names and the apothecary's."

A beat. "Or we sit here while the sun goes, and tomorrow nobody's paid at all — not Thorn, not us, not you."

He tips his chin at the lower sheds, mild. "And what's in the two you barred?"

cards.title: Persuasion: get Osric to let the case go with his question and his letter

screens.Sefa Marrin:
Bram settles his shield at his side and says that three weeks unpaid is no small matter, but the three of you are hired carriers: ninety gold between you on delivery, and nothing if you miss the buyer's coach at sunset. He remarks that the tools are stacked in good order and that he spoke too soon about trouble. Then he asks Hale who owes the wages, who took payment for the case, and what paper or letter would satisfy him enough to let you carry it out today.

Pell keeps watch on the yard while Hale speaks. He glances one time at the pair of lower sheds, both barred from the outside, then at the chimney, then murmurs to you and Bram that Hale is holding the case against the Gate, not against you, and that nobody bars sheds from outside to keep tools in. Stepping up behind Bram's shoulder, he tells Hale in an even voice that you are hired carry, not Thorn's counting-house, that nobody has brought his wages, and that the buyer's coach leaves Beregost at sunset. He offers to carry a sealed letter of Hale's with the case and put it in Thorn's hand, warns that sitting here means nobody gets paid, and asks what is in the two barred sheds.

Osric Hale listens to all of you without interrupting. He gives Bram's shield the same look as before, and takes longer over your face.

"Who owes them," he says. "House Vandarren. Gate patriars. Whitestone's theirs on paper." He reaches back without turning and takes a folded paper off a shelf just inside the door. He doesn't step out of the doorway. He holds it out at arm's length for Bram to read but doesn't let go.

It's a carter's order, in a clerk's neat hand on good paper: by the steward of House Vandarren, one case, sealed, of the rose salt from the low workings, to be held at Whitestone for M. Thorn of Beregost or her carriers. Account settled with the House's agent, A. Penn, at the Gate.

"Settled," Osric says. "Says so there. Three weeks back. Same week my wages stopped." He folds the paper into his apron. "So she paid. Penn took it. My lads got nothing."

He looks at Pell, then down at the two barred sheds, as if they had asked.

"Saws and the house's good irons in the near one. I barred it. The lads were angry, and angry men take things they'll hang for." His keys clink as his arms fold tighter. "Other's the old cutting-shed. Shut. Nobody works in it now."

He says nothing more about it.

Your offer is the one he is still turning over. He watches you the way he watched the cart, and you hold his eye, with Pell's offer of a letter and Bram's plain talk behind you.

cards.title: Persuasion: get Osric to let the case go with his question and his letter

presses.text:
The moment stretches, and then Osric Hale's arms come down from his chest. He draws a long breath through his nose, the way a man does when he has finished turning something over.

"Leave together or not at all," he echoes, but now he means the three of you, the case and his letter.

He steps back from the doorway only as far as he needs to, and gestures — not quite a wave — for you to come inside. "Then I'll write it. You'll wait while I do."

The house is small and spare: a worn table, one chair, a hearth burning low, a shelf of accounts and cupboards painted the same grey as the quarry dust on everything. The case already stands on the table, a squat wooden chest banded in iron, its seal a disc of hard blue wax stamped with a hooked thorn. Beside it, Hale sits, dips a nib, and writes with the slow care of a man who does not write often.

"I'll put your name," he says without looking up. "The dark-haired woman. And the case goes to no one else in Beregost but Thorn's own hand. If they turn you back at the shop, you keep it and send for me."

He writes a page, folds it twice, and seals it with plain brown wax and his thumb. He does not hand you the case yet.

"The letter's for Olek, in Little Calimshan — by the spice stair, ask for him." Osric holds the letter out to you. "He knows the whole account of it. If the Gate's still deaf by the full moon, Olek has what he needs to make the Vandarrens listen from a different side."

Only then does he stand, lift the case from the table by its handles, and set it into Bram's arms rather than yours, with a nod that might be to both of you.

"Watch the road down by Bram's Crossing," he says. "Some of my lads were talking of the old cutting-shed before they went. There are men in this country who'd take that case from a carrier for half what Thorn paid."

He steps out into the yard behind you, and the white light closes around you all again.

Where you are: Whitestone quarry yard, outside Warden Hale's house, the case in Bram's arms · Time: Day 1 · late morning

Round 3 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Thanks, that's a vivid take, and it reads like a scene you'd enjoy. Most of it, though, is the world's side of the table, so I'll treat it as a suggestion and not as what happened.

These parts are mine to decide, and the die decides them first: whether Osric gives way, what he says, what his house holds, what the seal looks like, and whether there is a letter at all. The same goes for Olek, the Vandarrens and the warning about the road. Where the case ends up is shared ground. Osric setting it into Bram's arms is fine for Osric to do, but whether Bram takes it is Bram's player's call.

One small point: a place called "Bram's Crossing" won't appear. It shares a name with Bram, and at this table people's names don't become places.

What stays yours is everything Sefa does: her words, her manner, where she stands, what she offers. If any of that is in what you wrote, send it as Sefa's own lines and I'll fold it in. Since the card was rolled with a particular approach in mind, tell me if your message changes what Sefa is actually doing.

Bram Halloway: I settle my shield at my side. “Three weeks unpaid is no small thing. But we’re hired carriers, Hale. Ninety gold between us on delivery, and nothing if we miss her buyer’s coach at sunset. I haven’t seen what she paid for the salt.”

I glance at the neatly stacked tools. “Your men left things in good order. I spoke too soon about trouble.”

Then I meet his eyes. “Who owes their wages, and who took payment for the case? If you’ve a bill or a letter tying the two together, let’s see it. What would satisfy you enough to let us carry it out today?”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa says, low, to Bram: "He's not a bandit. He's a man holding the only thing he has left to bargain with."

Then, to Osric, with her hands still open and her voice steady: "No one's paid us to take that case against your will. We don't carry wages from the Gate, and we won't pretend to. But we'll be in Beregost by sunset, and we can put your question directly to Maela Thorn — whether she knows whose pocket that money's sitting in. That's more than three weeks of letters have got you." She pauses, watching his face rather than his keys. "A sealed case kept here past nightfall buys nobody's supper, Master Hale. Let it go with us, and let your question go with it."

Pell Dunmore: Pell doesn't move his eyes from the yard while Hale talks. When the man finishes, he glances once at the two lower sheds — barred from outside — and then at the chimney, and only then at Hale.

Low, to Bram and Sefa, barely moving his mouth: "He's not holding the case against us. He's holding it against the Gate. We're just the nearest hands. And someone barred those two sheds from the outside before the crew left — you don't do that to keep tools in."

Then, a step behind Bram's shoulder, still not crowding the doorway, in an even, Lower City voice:

"Master Hale. We're hired carry, not her counting-house — she pays us on delivery, same as she's likely to pay you, which is why she's in a hurry and you're not. Nobody's sent us with your wages, and nobody's going to send them to a quarry that's gone quiet." A small nod toward the cart track. "Thorn's buyer leaves Beregost for the Gate at sunset. If you've got letters that want answering, that coach is the fastest road your complaint has had in three weeks. Write it, seal it, we carry it with the case and put it in her hand with the salt. You've got our names and the apothecary's."

A beat. "Or we sit here while the sun goes, and tomorrow nobody's paid at all — not Thorn, not us, not you."

He tips his chin at the lower sheds, mild. "And what's in the two you barred?"

It's a carter's order, written in a clerk's neat hand on good paper:

*By the steward of House Vandarren. One case, sealed, of the rose salt from the low workings, to be held at Whitestone for M. Thorn of Beregost or her carriers. Account settled with the House's agent, A. Penn, at the Gate.*

"Settled," Osric says. "Says so there. Three weeks back. Same week my wages stopped." He folds the paper and puts it in his apron. "So she paid. Penn took it. My lads got nothing."

He looks at Pell next, and then down at the two barred sheds, as if they had asked.

"Saws and the house's good irons in the near one. I barred it. The lads were angry, and angry men take things they'll hang for." His keys clink as his arms fold tighter. "Other's the old cutting-shed. Shut. Nobody works in it now."

He doesn't say anything more about it.

Sefa's offer is the one he's still turning over. He watches her the way he watched the cart, and she holds his eye with Pell's offer of a letter and Bram's plain talk behind her.

Sefa's even voice does it. She hasn't promised him wages and she isn't pretending to be anything she's not, and in the end that's what he can't argue with. Something in his shoulders gives a little, though his arms stay folded.

"Right," Osric says. "You carry my question. And my letter, to Thorn's own hand. Not to her boy, not left on the counter." He jerks his chin at Pell. "You said it. Fastest road it's had."

He steps back into the house at last, and the doorway opens on one room: a cot, a hearth with a low fire and a kettle, a table, and a thick tally-book bound in canvas lying open on it. On the floor under the table, out of reach of the hearth, sits a squat iron-cornered case about the size of a bread box. It's bound with cord, and there's a blob of grey wax on the knot with a house seal pressed into it.

Osric sits down at the table and pulls an inkpot over. "One of you signs the book for it. Your name, Thorn's name, the day. I don't let house stock walk off on a nod."

He dips the pen and starts writing slowly on a torn-out leaf, in a heavy, careful hand. He doesn't look up.

"I walk to Beregost myself at noon. Lads are drinking there on credit they haven't got. Somebody ought to stand with them when Thorn's answer comes back."

The pen scratches on. Out in the yard the dust lies still in the heat, and the two barred sheds stand shut in the sun at the bottom of the cut.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa waits for Osric to finish writing, then says, "I'll sign for it." She steps just inside the doorway, not crowding him, and signs her name in the tally-book when he turns it toward her. "Sefa Marrin. I'll carry your letter to Maela Thorn's own hand, and if she gives an answer before you reach Beregost, I'll find you there."

She glances once at the case — not greedily, but as a hospice novice would regard something that must arrive whole. "Is there anything else a carrier should know between here and the shop?" she asks. "You said the lads talked of the old cutting-shed. If there's ground we should avoid, or a signal they know you by, it'd be worth more than coin to hear it now."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays in the doorway a moment longer than he needs to, then steps in sideways — he doesn't like to stand in doorways with his back to a yard. He doesn't go to the table. He goes to the case, crouches, and looks before he touches: the cord, how the knot's tied, whether the wax sits on the knot or beside it, whether the seal's edge has the little lifted lip you get when someone warms it and sets it back. Then he lifts the case an inch by one iron corner to feel the weight and whether anything shifts inside. He's quiet about it, the way he'd check a lock before trusting it.

"Seal's a Vandarren house seal?" he asks Hale, without looking up. "Same as on your order?"

To Bram, low: "You sign. Your name's the one that's been on a caravan manifest before, and I'd sooner mine stayed out of a Gate house's book." A glance at the open tally-book, not to read it, just to see how many pages back the last entry is.

Then, still quiet, to Sefa and Bram: "We've got maybe nine hours of light and six of road. Case, letter, and go. Whatever's in the cutting-shed is his business and the lads'. We're paid for a box."

He stands, and to Hale, plain: "You walk at noon, you'll be an hour behind us. If you want it, we'll find you at whatever tavern the lads are drinking in before we hand Thorn her answer, so you hear it first." He leaves it there — an offer, not a promise he'll chase.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Thorn’s own hand,” I agree. “And we’ll ask her for an answer. That much we can promise.”

I step inside and read the tally-book’s receipt before signing, making sure it records collection of one sealed case for Maela Thorn, not an inspection of its contents. I check the cord, wax and corners for existing damage without disturbing the seal, then put my name and the day beside hers.

“If you’re nearly ready, walk back with us. Better company than your letters have had.” I nod toward the case. “Anything we need to know about carrying rose salt—keep it dry, keep it upright?”

scenes.narration:
Osric's pen keeps scratching while they talk. He writes slowly and doesn't stop to reread. When the letter is done he pushes it to one side, pulls the tally-book in front of him and writes a fresh line in the same heavy hand. Then he turns the book round on the table.

*One case rose salt, low working. Sealed with house stock seal, wax whole. Collected for M. Thorn of Beregost by her carriers.*

Bram reads it before he picks up the pen. The line says *collected* and nothing about the case being opened or looked into. Sefa signs first, *Sefa Marrin*, and Bram writes his name and the day under hers. Osric takes a pinch of white stone dust from a chipped dish beside the inkpot, scatters it over the wet ink and tips the book to shake it off. That's the only blotting sand he keeps.

Pell crouches by the case while they sign. The cord is good hemp, crossed twice over the lid and tied off in a carter's knot. The wax sits on the knot itself, a thumb-thick grey lump with a single clean impression. Its edges are dull and grained with dust, with no shine and no lifted lip. Nobody has warmed it and pressed it again. When he lifts one iron corner an inch, the case is far heavier than a box that size should be, twenty-odd pounds, like a block of stone. Tipping it sets something shifting dry and coarse inside, like salt settling in a sack. A few grains of pale pink dust are caught in the crease where the lid meets the iron corner.

"House stock seal," Osric says, without turning. He touches a small brass seal hanging among the keys at his belt. "Mine to keep. Steward has its twin. Every case that leaves here gets it." A moment later he adds, "Order's signed, not sealed. Steward doesn't waste wax on me."

The tally-book is open far enough for Pell to see it without reading. It runs thick with one line a day, loads of stone counted off in fives, page after page back toward the front cover. The line above the one Osric just wrote is short. *Noon. Crew off. 3 wks owed.*

Then Osric answers Sefa. "Didn't say the lads talked of it." He lets that sit a moment. "Keep to the track. Don't cut across the lip to save the bend. Ground's been worked under since before my time. Old drifts. Some of them took water." He pulls the letter back in front of him. "Lads won't need a sign. Tell them Hale's coming. They'll stay put for that."

He gives Bram the same flat attention. "Dry. Damp makes it cake, and Thorn'll call it spoiled. Upright doesn't matter. Don't open it." His answer to the other question is just as short. "No. Noon. House to shut. And I'll not walk into Beregost at Thorn's back like I'm her man."

He looks at Pell last. "Burning Wizard. Credit's easiest there." He doesn't thank him.

He folds the letter in three and drips a little plain tallow from the candle-end on the table onto the fold. He doesn't press his house seal into it. He holds the letter out across the table to Sefa, and it goes into her hand. Then he hooks a boot behind the case and slides it out from under the table onto the open floor between the three of them.

"It's yours. Book says so."

He sits back with his hands flat on the table. The low fire ticks in the hearth and the kettle has gone quiet. Through the open shutters the sun is still climbing over the white faces of the cut, and the lifting frame's shadow is drawing in across the yard.

Your narration:
<<<
Osric's pen keeps scratching while they talk. He writes slowly and doesn't stop to reread. When the letter is done he pushes it to one side, pulls the tally-book in front of him and writes a fresh line in the same heavy hand. Then he turns the book round on the table.

*One case rose salt, low working. Sealed with house stock seal, wax whole. Collected for M. Thorn of Beregost by her carriers.*

Bram reads it before he picks up the pen. The line says *collected* and nothing about the case being opened or looked into. Sefa signs first, *Sefa Marrin*, and Bram writes his name and the day under hers. Osric takes a pinch of white stone dust from a chipped dish beside the inkpot, scatters it over the wet ink and tips the book to shake it off. That's the only blotting sand he keeps.

Pell crouches by the case while they sign. The cord is good hemp, crossed twice over the lid and tied off in a carter's knot. The wax sits on the knot itself, a thumb-thick grey lump with a single clean impression. Its edges are dull and grained with dust, with no shine and no lifted lip. Nobody has warmed it and pressed it again. When he lifts one iron corner an inch, the case is far heavier than a box that size should be, twenty-odd pounds, like a block of stone. Tipping it sets something shifting dry and coarse inside, like salt settling in a sack. A few grains of pale pink dust are caught in the crease where the lid meets the iron corner.

"House stock seal," Osric says, without turning. He touches a small brass seal hanging among the keys at his belt. "Mine to keep. Steward has its twin. Every case that leaves here gets it." A moment later he adds, "Order's signed, not sealed. Steward doesn't waste wax on me."

The tally-book is open far enough for Pell to see it without reading. It runs thick with one line a day, loads of stone counted off in fives, page after page back toward the front cover. The line above the one Osric just wrote is short. *Noon. Crew off. 3 wks owed.*

Then Osric answers Sefa. "Didn't say the lads talked of it." He lets that sit a moment. "Keep to the track. Don't cut across the lip to save the bend. Ground's been worked under since before my time. Old drifts. Some of them took water." He pulls the letter back in front of him. "Lads won't need a sign. Tell them Hale's coming. They'll stay put for that."

He gives Bram the same flat attention. "Dry. Damp makes it cake, and Thorn'll call it spoiled. Upright doesn't matter. Don't open it." His answer to the other question is just as short. "No. Noon. House to shut. And I'll not walk into Beregost at Thorn's back like I'm her man."

He looks at Pell last. "Burning Wizard. Credit's easiest there." He doesn't thank him.

He folds the letter in three and drips a little plain tallow from the candle-end on the table onto the fold. He doesn't press his house seal into it. He holds the letter out across the table to Sefa, and it goes into her hand. Then he hooks a boot behind the case and slides it out from under the table onto the open floor between the three of them.

"It's yours. Book says so."

He sits back with his hands flat on the table. The low fire ticks in the hearth and the kettle has gone quiet. Through the open shutters the sun is still climbing over the white faces of the cut, and the lifting frame's shadow is drawing in across the yard.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell nods once to Hale — the only thanks the man's going to accept — and picks the case up by its iron corners, testing the heft again. Twenty-odd pounds; nothing for a mile, a shoulder-ache by the sixth.

"Bram, you've got the back for it, but a man with a shield and a box has no hands. I'll carry." He unslings his pack, pulls out the silk rope, and rigs a quick cradle round the case — two turns under, one over the lid clear of the wax, a loop long enough to go across his chest so it rides on his back and leaves both hands free. He wraps the bedroll's canvas round it first against damp and dust. Fast work; he's done it with heavier things off higher ledges.

"We go the track, not the lip. Hale says the ground's hollow and I believe a man who's walked it twenty years." A glance back at the two barred sheds as he settles the weight. Not his box, not his pay. He lets it go.

To Sefa, quiet: "Letter stays on you. Thorn's own hand, like he said — we don't put it down anywhere." To Bram: "You in front, me middle with the case, Sefa behind. If anything's on that track that wasn't this morning, I want to see it before it sees the box."

Then, at the door, to Hale: "Burning Wizard. We'll be there." And he steps out into the glare and starts down toward the cart track.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Dry, sealed, and keep to the track. Understood. Safe road, Hale.”

I wrap the case in my bedroll against dust and splashes, then lash it securely to my pack, leaving the sealed cord untouched. I settle the load before heading out.

“Burning Wizard if we have an answer for you,” I add at the door.

Outside, I say quietly to Pell and Sefa, “Let’s earn our pay. No shortcuts over old workings.”

I start back along the cart track, watching the footing and the road ahead.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa folds the letter carefully into an inner pocket beside her prayer beads before she answers.

"The book may say so, but I'd rather the man who kept it say so too. Thank you, Master Hale." She says it plainly, without lingering, and steps back out of the doorway to leave him his house.

Outside, she studies the yard again — not the cut, but the way they came, the treeline past the track, and the long white road toward Beregost. "Keep to the track," she says quietly to Pell and Bram, "as he said. I'll carry the letter. Bram already has the case. Pell, if it comes to trouble, I'd rather you saw it before it saw us."

She turns once more to Osric, framed in the doorway. "When I find you in Beregost, I'll ask for Master Hale at the Burning Wizard. If Maela Thorn has an answer first, I'll bring it there."

scenes.narration:
Pell's hands are quicker than Bram's. By the time Bram has shaken out his bedroll and knelt for the case, there's nothing on the boards. The case is already off the floor and wrapped in the canvas of Pell's own bedroll, with silk rope going twice under it and once over the lid, clear of the grey wax. A long loop of the rope runs across Pell's chest, so the case rides high and square on his back. It's heavy the way stone is heavy, and the salt shifts inside with a dry whisper when he settles it.

Sefa tucks the letter into an inner pocket next to her prayer beads. Osric hears her thanks without turning round, and her line about the man who kept the book saying it too.

"Said it," he says. That's all.

He's already getting up from the table. He rakes the low fire into a heap of ash with the poker and pushes the kettle to the back of the hearth. Then he crosses to the side window, the shuttered one, and checks the bar on it with his palm, the way a man checks a thing he checked yesterday. Bram's *safe road* gets a short nod. Pell's *Burning Wizard* gets nothing at all, and Bram's after it gets the same.

"Go on, then," Osric says from inside the room. "Light's wasting."

The door shuts behind them with a sound of wood on stone. A moment later the bolt goes across.

The yard is brighter now and the dust hotter underfoot. Bram goes first with his shield on his arm, and Sefa comes last with the letter against her ribs. They pass the lower cut, where the hammers still lie head to head and the wedges sit in their neat stack. They pass the half-loaded cart with its traces hanging over the shaft, and the two barred sheds at the bottom of the cut. The near shed has a newer bar, pale wood, cut not long ago. The far one, the old cutting-shed, has a bar grey with age, and the dust has drifted against its door sill and lies there unbroken.

Past the sheds the cart track leaves the yard and drops off the shelf of the workings. It swings out in a long, slow bend around the lip of the lower cut, wide enough for a stone cart, the ground packed hard and white by years of wheels. Across the mouth of the bend runs a much narrower footpath, straight over the lip. It would save a few hundred feet. Grass has grown back into it, and halfway along, the turf sags in a shallow dip as if something underneath had settled. The churned band of the crew's bootprints goes nowhere near it. A dozen men and a mule kept to the long way round, every one of them.

Behind the party, the thread of smoke above Osric's chimney is already thinning as the banked fire dies. Ahead, the long white road runs down toward Beregost between dry grass and scrub oak, with the sun not yet at its height.

The yard is brighter now and the dust hotter underfoot. Bram goes first with his shield on his arm, and Sefa comes last with the letter against her ribs. They pass the lower cut, where the hammers still lie head to head and the wedges sit in their neat stack. They pass the half-loaded cart with its traces hanging over the shaft, and the two barred sheds at the bottom of the cut. The near shed has a newer bar, pale wood, cut not long ago. The far one, the old cutting-shed, has a bar grey with age, and the dust has drifted against its door sill and lies there unbroken.

Past the sheds the cart track leaves the yard and drops off the shelf of the workings. It swings out in a long, slow bend around the lip of the lower cut, wide enough for a stone cart, the ground packed hard and white by years of wheels. Across the mouth of the bend runs a much narrower footpath, straight over the lip. It would save a few hundred feet. Grass has grown back into it, and halfway along, the turf sags in a shallow dip as if something underneath had settled. The churned band of the crew's bootprints goes nowhere near it. A dozen men and a mule kept to the long way round, every one of them.

Behind the party, the thread of smoke above Osric's chimney is already thinning as the banked fire dies. Ahead, the long white road runs down toward Beregost between dry grass and scrub oak, with the sun not yet at its height.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep to the broad wheel-packed track around the bend, following the route the crew and mule took.

“Sing out when you want that load traded, Pell. Six hours is a long way to prove a point.”

I set a steady walking pace toward Beregost, keeping an eye on the scrub ahead and either side of the road. No detours unless something gives us cause to stop.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the others draw a few paces ahead, then stops only long enough to study the footpath across the lip. The grass-grown dip holds her eye a moment too long.

"The crew kept to the long way," she says, pitching her voice to reach Pell and Bram, not the empty yard. "Twelve men and the mule, every print. I don't mean to be the one who finds out what that turf knows."

She adjusts the strap of her pack, settles the letter against her ribs with one flat hand, and falls in at the rear as they take the long bend around the cut. As they walk, she keeps her eyes moving: the road ahead, the dry scrub on either side, and every now and then a look back at the smoke above the quarry.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gives the footpath one look as they pass its mouth — the sagging turf, the grass grown back, a dozen men and a mule who all knew better — and keeps his boots on the hard white of the cart track.

"That's the one," he says to the others, nodding at the dip without slowing. "Settles under you and you're in an old drift with twenty pound of salt on your back and no rope to climb. We take the bend."

He settles the case higher on his shoulders and falls into the long, even stride of a man who has a half-day of road and means to arrive. Every so often, without making a show of it, he checks behind: the thinning smoke, the quarry shelf, the track they've walked — anyone coming down after them, anyone who was waiting for the carriers to leave with the box. The dust on the cutting-shed's sill was unbroken; whatever Hale isn't saying about that shed, it's been shut a long while, and that's a Vandarren matter, not his.

To Sefa, after a while, quiet: "If Thorn's paid and Penn pocketed it, that's a Gate house's steward with his hand in the till, and we're the ones carrying the proof down a road. I'd like to be in Beregost before anyone thinks that through." He watches the scrub oak on either side as he says it.

He keeps the pace brisk and steady — no stops till the sun's well past noon, and then only for water.

scenes.narration:
Past the mouth of the footpath the cart track swings out along the lip of the lower cut. The surface is packed so hard from years of iron-shod wheels that it rings faintly under a boot. Bram sets the pace in front with his shield on his arm, watching the scrub. Pell walks in the middle with the case riding square on his back. Sefa comes last, and when she looks back the smoke above the quarry is only a smudge now.

Under the bend the ground sounds wrong.

It isn't loud, just a dull wooden note under Pell's left heel. A moment later there's a creak like a ship's timber. A crack runs out across the white crust from his foot, toward the edge of the cut. The road is a little softer here, on the outer side where the wheels never quite reached. Then the crust opens up under him, and Pell goes down through it in a rush of chalk, rotten board and dust.

The case saves itself. As Pell drops, the canvas bundle on his back hits the broken end of an old pit-prop that juts out of the hole's wall a foot below the road. The silk rope catches on it and holds. The loop across his chest goes tight, scrapes up over his collarbone and jaw, and tears free over his head. Then he's falling with nothing on his back. The case swings once on the rope above him and comes to rest hanging from the timber, out of the water.

He lands hard. The bottom is eight feet down, under chest-deep water so cold it knocks the breath out of him before the stone does. His hip and shoulder hit rock under the water. It's a heavy, jarring blow, the kind that will be purple tomorrow, but nothing gives in him that shouldn't. A moment later the collapse comes down after him: dust, board, a slab of the road's crust, and from the wall beside him something much heavier. A squared block of white stone, two feet on a side, slides out of the wall where the fall has torn it loose. It rolls once in the water and settles across his left leg below the knee. It pins the leg flat against the bottom. It doesn't crush it, but it holds it the way a vice holds.

Then the dust thins in the shaft of daylight from the hole.

Pell is in an old drift. It's a low tunnel cut square into the white rock and roofed with grey timbers. It runs off into the dark in both directions, and the water fills it to a level line. Somewhere back along it, water is trickling steadily, the way a seep sounds when it never stops. The water around his chest is clear and very cold, and a faint pink dust drifts on its surface where the road came down.

The block lies beside his face, half out of the water and turned up by the fall. Its upper face isn't rough quarry stone. It's dressed smooth, and in the light from above there's a carving on it. It's a disc with straight rays running out from it, like a sun coming up, cut deep and clean. A ring of small chisel marks runs round it, short strokes and notches set in groups, some crossed, some single. There's old grey plaster crusted along one edge of the block, as though it had been set into the wall and mortared there.

Up on the road, Bram has spun round at the crack. A ragged hole has opened at the outer edge of the track, four feet across, and white dust is still pouring up out of it. Sefa sees it from the rear: one step Pell was walking, and the next he was gone. Through the hole they can both see the silk rope pulled taut over the broken prop, the canvas bundle turning slowly on it a few feet down, and below that the dark water with Pell in it, his head and shoulders above the surface and a pale block lying across where his leg should be. The edge of the hole is still crumbling. A cake of crust the size of a hand breaks off as they look and drops past the case into the water.

The sun is still climbing in the east. It isn't noon yet, and behind them the quarry is silent.

 Neither action needed a roll: both were simple walking and watching, and the turn covered them, so here they are in full.

Before the ground went, Bram had kept the steady pace on the wheel-packed track that the crew and the mule took. The scrub oak on both sides was empty: no movement, no glint, no fresh tracks off the road, and nothing ahead on the white road down toward Beregost. Sefa had looked hard at the grassy dip on the footpath, enough to see the turf sagging over a hollow and every one of the crew's prints going round it. Since then she had kept looking back, and nobody followed them down from the quarry shelf. All that showed was Osric's chimney, its smoke thinning to nothing. Nothing on the road or in the scrub would have made them stop. Only the ground did.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa's voice cuts through the dust before it settles: "Pell, don't kick — the stone shifts. Lie still. I can heal you from here, but you'll waste it if you're thrashing."

She stays back from the lip, spreads her feet, and turns half toward Bram. "Bram, on your belly before the edge. Anchor to something solid — one of the scrub roots, not the crust. I'll guide a rope to him from up here." She draws a slow breath, flattening the fear into something useful. "The case is hung on the prop — that's holding. We get Pell first."

Then she lets the first warmth come up from behind the letter against her ribs, not the Lantern's full light, but a single glowing thread: she sends two d6 of healing light down into the dark water, toward the man she can see but not touch.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell holds very still for a three-count, the way you do when you don't yet know what's broken. Breath. Fingers. Toes — the left ones move, under the stone. Good. Then he spits chalk and tips his head back to the hole.

"Don't come to the edge!" Not loud — the roof's timber and he doesn't trust it. "It's still going. Get back from it. Both of you." A beat to let them. "I'm in one piece. Hip and shoulder, nothing broken. Left leg's under a block, pinned, not crushed. Case is hanging off a prop a foot under the road — it's dry, don't touch it yet. Water's chest-deep and there's a seep running somewhere, so I'd like to not be here long."

He gets his hands under the water and feels along the block's edge where it meets his shin — how it's sitting, whether it's bedded on rock or on loose fall. Rock, he's not shifting two feet of dressed stone with Strength like his. Loose fall, he can dig the leg out from under rather than lift the block off. He starts scooping at whatever's under his calf, slow, working the leg a quarter-inch at a time, bracing his free foot against the block to push rather than pull. If it won't give, he'll try wedging a dagger-hilt and a chunk of fallen board under the near corner for a hair of lift.

Up at the hole, while he works: "Bram — the case is on *my* rope. Don't cut it loose to get me; I'd sooner it hang there till I'm up. Have you got rope? Or the cart's traces, back in the yard — they were unbuckled, not cut. Hale's got rope too, he'll be awake another hour. Sefa, you've got light that heals — if you can do that from up there, I'd take it. If you have to come down, come down the far wall from the fall, not through the hole."

Only then does he look properly at the block beside his face — the sun-disc, the notched ring, the old plaster. He wipes a wet thumb across the chisel marks.

"Hale said the ground was worked under since before his time." Quiet, mostly to himself. "He didn't say by who." He doesn't touch it again. One problem at a time.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell! We’ve got you. Is your leg pinned?”

I move toward the inner side of the track, away from the crumbling outer edge, and set my shield down. I pull out my hempen rope and tie a broad loop in one end.

“Sefa, call Hale! Tell him the track’s fallen in—we need help and a long timber.”

Staying back from the broken lip, I lower myself flat to spread my weight and try to feed the loop down within Pell’s reach.

“Under your arms if you can. Keep your head up. We’ll worry about the box later.”

I brace on intact ground and take up slack to help support him above the water, without trying to wrench him free of the stone.

cards.title: Strength (Athletics), Strength +0, unproficient: dig the leg out from under the block and push free

presses.text:
Pell's hands come up out of the water with nothing but chalk-mud under the nails. The leg's bedded on rock, not fall — nobody's digging it out. He stops before he does the stupid thing and starts kicking.

"Not moving," he calls up, flat. "Block's sitting on stone, I'm just pushing water around. Sefa's right. New plan."

He takes Bram's loop as it comes down and gets it under his arms, snug across the chest, then gives it a tug to show it's seated. "That's me on your rope, Bram. Don't haul yet — if you pull me straight up with the leg under this, you'll keep the leg." He reaches for the biggest piece of fallen board within arm's length — a chunk of the road's old planking — and works one end of it down under the near corner of the block, where the stone sits proudest off the bottom. His dagger goes under the board's heel as a fulcrum.

"Here's how it goes. I lever the corner — a finger's width is all I need. The second it lifts, you take up the slack hard and I kick the leg out toward you, away from the block. If it drops back, it drops back on bottom, not on me. Count of three on my word, not before." A breath. "And Sefa — if that light's for me, now's good. I'll want the leg working when it's out."

He gets both hands on the board, braces his free boot against the block's flank, and waits for Bram's rope to go taut.
presses.reply:
Got it, and thanks. Pell's lines and what Pell does with his own hands stand as written: he calls up that the leg isn't moving, asks Bram not to haul yet, works a board under the block's near corner with his dagger as a fulcrum, sets the count of three on his word, braces his boot, and asks Sefa for the light. All of that is yours.

A few parts belong to other people, so I'll treat them as suggestions:

- **What the die did, and why the leg won't come.** The card you pressed [Onward] on decides that, and the narration tells it next as an event. The reason it gives may not be "bedded on rock". Read it as Pell's guess until the story confirms it.
- **Bram's loop and Bram hauling.** Bram's player decides whether a rope comes down and when it goes taut. Pell can ask for it and set the count. He can't assume the rope is already round his chest.
- **Sefa's light.** Sefa's player decides whether she spends Healing Light and on whom. Pell's "now's good" is a request she hears.
- **"Sefa's right."** That's Pell's line, and it stands. If it points at something Sefa says this round, it lands once her player has said it.

The lever is a fresh attempt with a new plan. It comes after this check, not inside it, so it plays out in the next round alongside whatever Bram and Sefa do. Once the three of you are working on the block together, the story will say plainly what it takes and how long it runs against the sky. The board, the fulcrum and two people on it all count when it does.

scenes.narration:
Sefa's voice reaches down the hole, low and level. Then a thread of warm, pale light runs out of her hand and down past the dangling case.

The light falls straight and steady and reaches Pell in the water. It's warm in a way the drift isn't. It runs into his hip and shoulder, and the deep ache goes out of both, all of it, the way a cramp lets go. Whatever the fall knocked out of him, Sefa's light has put back. For a moment the cold seems to stand a little farther off. Then the glow fades on the water and the cold closes in again.

Pell lies still for his three-count. His toes move under the stone. He calls up his warning, and on the road both of them hear it: *it's still going, get back.* While he talks, his hands go under the water to the block.

What he finds is bad. The block is lying across the slope of the fall, not flat on the bottom. Its far end rests on solid floor, dressed rock cut level by the old miners. Its near end, the end on his shin, sits on the loose heap that came down with the road: lumps of crust, splinters of rotten board, wet chalk. His calf is pressed down into that heap. So he digs. He scoops out a handful from under his calf, then another, and pushes off the block's face with his free foot.

It goes wrong quickly. In the water the chalk turns to paste, and every handful he pulls out lets the next lot slump in after it. The block doesn't wait for him either. He feels it lower itself into the gap he's dug, a slow half-inch of a weight far heavier than he is, until it's pressing harder than before. He shoves anyway. His knee twists against the stone and something in it wrenches hot, and the leg stays where it is. He gets the dagger-hilt and a piece of board under the near corner, and both sink into the paste without lifting the block a hair. The leg is no freer than when he started, it throbs now, and the water around him has turned milky with stirred chalk.

The water also shows him what it would take. Lying there with his hands on it, a man who knows how weight sits can read the whole job. Somebody has to get a lever under the block's near end and lift it. An old pit-prop lies along the drift wall six feet from him, a grey beam as long as a man, fallen long ago and half under water. With that lever, a rope from above to take its weight, and somebody down in the water digging the paste out from under his calf while the lift holds, the block will come up. But only an inch at a time, with the water bailed down every so often to get at the bottom, and the rubble shifting each time it moves. Two people working without a break would have him out at about sunset. One person can't do it at all, because one person can't hold the lever and dig at once. And the sun hasn't reached its height yet. The road to Beregost is a good six hours. If one of them took the case and left now, Maela would have it with hours to spare. If two stay to dig, the case is still hanging here when her buyer's coach leaves the town.

Bram meanwhile has backed off to the inner side of the track, away from the crumbling lip. He lays his shield face-down on the packed white ground and ties a broad loop in the end of his hempen rope. The nearest solid thing is a scrub oak growing out of the bank on the inner side of the track, about fifteen feet up from the hole. Its roots grip the hillside, not the crust. Bram lies flat a body's length back from the broken edge, so his weight is spread on ground that still rings hard under his palm, and works the loop forward. It drops past Pell's canvas bundle, clear of the silk rope and the prop, and slaps the water beside Pell's shoulder. Pell gets it over his head and under his arms. Bram takes up the slack until it's taut, enough to carry part of Pell's weight and keep his head up without pulling on the leg. The rope creaks over the lip. A little more crust breaks off where it bites and patters into the water.

With the rope holding him up, Pell can look at the block beside his face. He wipes the plaster dust off the ring of chisel marks with his wet thumb. The marks are short strokes in little groups, some crossed through and some standing alone. They look a lot like the tally in Hale's book on the table this morning, loads counted off in fives and struck through. But Hale's book was counting stone. Nobody counts anything around a carved sun. Where the block tore out of the wall there's now a square socket two feet across, just above the water. At its back, where there should be raw rock, there's a flat, smooth face of old grey plaster, laid on by hand.

Back up the track, past the sheds, the warden's house stands shut with its bolt across. Its chimney gives off a last faint wisp and then nothing. In the drift, the seep trickles on in the dark. The waterline on the white wall sits a finger's width above the dark stain it was at a few minutes ago.

You set your shield down face-down on the packed white ground and tie a broad loop in the end of your hempen rope. You ask Sefa to call Hale and tell him the track has fallen in and you need help and a long timber.

Sefa's voice goes down the hole, low and level. She tells Pell not to kick, because the stone shifts, and to lie still. She says she can heal him from where she is. She tells you to get on your belly before the edge and anchor to something solid, a scrub root rather than the crust, and says Pell comes first because the case is held on the prop.

The nearest solid thing is a scrub oak growing out of the bank on the inner side of the track, about fifteen feet up from the hole. Its roots grip the hillside, not the crust. You lie flat a body's length back from the broken edge, on ground that still rings hard under your palm, and work the loop forward.

A thread of warm, pale light runs out of Sefa's hand and down past the dangling case. It falls straight and steady, and you see it reach Pell in the water and fade. Pell lies still, then calls up that the ground is still going and you should both get back.

The loop drops past Pell's canvas bundle, clear of the silk rope and the prop, and slaps the water beside his shoulder. He gets it over his head and under his arms. You take up the slack until it's taut, enough to carry part of his weight and keep his head up without pulling on the leg. The rope creaks over the lip. A little more crust breaks off where it bites and patters into the water.

Down there Pell works at the block with his hands under the water, and chalk clouds the water until it turns milky. He stays pinned. Then, held up by your rope, he wipes his thumb across the chisel marks on the block beside his face.

Back up the track, past the sheds, the warden's house stands shut with its bolt across. Its chimney gives off a last faint wisp and then nothing. The seep trickles on in the dark, and the waterline on the white wall sits a finger's width above where it was a few minutes ago.

relay.request:
Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
In this scene: Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway.
Write the screens of, in this order: Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Sefa Marrin: Sefa's voice cuts through the dust before it settles: "Pell, don't kick — the stone shifts. Lie still. I can heal you from here, but you'll waste it if you're thrashing."

She stays back from the lip, spreads her feet, and turns half toward Bram. "Bram, on your belly before the edge. Anchor to something solid — one of the scrub roots, not the crust. I'll guide a rope to him from up here." She draws a slow breath, flattening the fear into something useful. "The case is hung on the prop — that's holding. We get Pell first."

Then she lets the first warmth come up from behind the letter against her ribs, not the Lantern's full light, but a single glowing thread: she sends two d6 of healing light down into the dark water, toward the man she can see but not touch.

Pell Dunmore: Pell holds very still for a three-count, the way you do when you don't yet know what's broken. Breath. Fingers. Toes — the left ones move, under the stone. Good. Then he spits chalk and tips his head back to the hole.

"Don't come to the edge!" Not loud — the roof's timber and he doesn't trust it. "It's still going. Get back from it. Both of you." A beat to let them. "I'm in one piece. Hip and shoulder, nothing broken. Left leg's under a block, pinned, not crushed. Case is hanging off a prop a foot under the road — it's dry, don't touch it yet. Water's chest-deep and there's a seep running somewhere, so I'd like to not be here long."

He gets his hands under the water and feels along the block's edge where it meets his shin — how it's sitting, whether it's bedded on rock or on loose fall. Rock, he's not shifting two feet of dressed stone with Strength like his. Loose fall, he can dig the leg out from under rather than lift the block off. He starts scooping at whatever's under his calf, slow, working the leg a quarter-inch at a time, bracing his free foot against the block to push rather than pull. If it won't give, he'll try wedging a dagger-hilt and a chunk of fallen board under the near corner for a hair of lift.

Up at the hole, while he works: "Bram — the case is on *my* rope. Don't cut it loose to get me; I'd sooner it hang there till I'm up. Have you got rope? Or the cart's traces, back in the yard — they were unbuckled, not cut. Hale's got rope too, he'll be awake another hour. Sefa, you've got light that heals — if you can do that from up there, I'd take it. If you have to come down, come down the far wall from the fall, not through the hole."

Only then does he look properly at the block beside his face — the sun-disc, the notched ring, the old plaster. He wipes a wet thumb across the chisel marks.

"Hale said the ground was worked under since before his time." Quiet, mostly to himself. "He didn't say by who." He doesn't touch it again. One problem at a time.

Bram Halloway: “Pell! We’ve got you. Is your leg pinned?”

I move toward the inner side of the track, away from the crumbling outer edge, and set my shield down. I pull out my hempen rope and tie a broad loop in one end.

“Sefa, call Hale! Tell him the track’s fallen in—we need help and a long timber.”

Staying back from the broken lip, I lower myself flat to spread my weight and try to feed the loop down within Pell’s reach.

“Under your arms if you can. Keep your head up. We’ll worry about the box later.”

I brace on intact ground and take up slack to help support him above the water, without trying to wrench him free of the stone.
>>>

Your narration:
<<<
Sefa's voice reaches down the hole, low and level. Then a thread of warm, pale light runs out of her hand and down past the dangling case.

The light falls straight and steady and reaches Pell in the water. It's warm in a way the drift isn't. It runs into his hip and shoulder, and the deep ache goes out of both, all of it, the way a cramp lets go. Whatever the fall knocked out of him, Sefa's light has put back. For a moment the cold seems to stand a little farther off. Then the glow fades on the water and the cold closes in again.

Pell lies still for his three-count. His toes move under the stone. He calls up his warning, and on the road both of them hear it: *it's still going, get back.* While he talks, his hands go under the water to the block.

What he finds is bad. The block is lying across the slope of the fall, not flat on the bottom. Its far end rests on solid floor, dressed rock cut level by the old miners. Its near end, the end on his shin, sits on the loose heap that came down with the road: lumps of crust, splinters of rotten board, wet chalk. His calf is pressed down into that heap. So he digs. He scoops out a handful from under his calf, then another, and pushes off the block's face with his free foot.

It goes wrong quickly. In the water the chalk turns to paste, and every handful he pulls out lets the next lot slump in after it. The block doesn't wait for him either. He feels it lower itself into the gap he's dug, a slow half-inch of a weight far heavier than he is, until it's pressing harder than before. He shoves anyway. His knee twists against the stone and something in it wrenches hot, and the leg stays where it is. He gets the dagger-hilt and a piece of board under the near corner, and both sink into the paste without lifting the block a hair. The leg is no freer than when he started, it throbs now, and the water around him has turned milky with stirred chalk.

The water also shows him what it would take. Lying there with his hands on it, a man who knows how weight sits can read the whole job. Somebody has to get a lever under the block's near end and lift it. An old pit-prop lies along the drift wall six feet from him, a grey beam as long as a man, fallen long ago and half under water. With that lever, a rope from above to take its weight, and somebody down in the water digging the paste out from under his calf while the lift holds, the block will come up. But only an inch at a time, with the water bailed down every so often to get at the bottom, and the rubble shifting each time it moves. Two people working without a break would have him out at about sunset. One person can't do it at all, because one person can't hold the lever and dig at once. And the sun hasn't reached its height yet. The road to Beregost is a good six hours. If one of them took the case and left now, Maela would have it with hours to spare. If two stay to dig, the case is still hanging here when her buyer's coach leaves the town.

Bram meanwhile has backed off to the inner side of the track, away from the crumbling lip. He lays his shield face-down on the packed white ground and ties a broad loop in the end of his hempen rope. The nearest solid thing is a scrub oak growing out of the bank on the inner side of the track, about fifteen feet up from the hole. Its roots grip the hillside, not the crust. Bram lies flat a body's length back from the broken edge, so his weight is spread on ground that still rings hard under his palm, and works the loop forward. It drops past Pell's canvas bundle, clear of the silk rope and the prop, and slaps the water beside Pell's shoulder. Pell gets it over his head and under his arms. Bram takes up the slack until it's taut, enough to carry part of Pell's weight and keep his head up without pulling on the leg. The rope creaks over the lip. A little more crust breaks off where it bites and patters into the water.

With the rope holding him up, Pell can look at the block beside his face. He wipes the plaster dust off the ring of chisel marks with his wet thumb. The marks are short strokes in little groups, some crossed through and some standing alone. They look a lot like the tally in Hale's book on the table this morning, loads counted off in fives and struck through. But Hale's book was counting stone. Nobody counts anything around a carved sun. Where the block tore out of the wall there's now a square socket two feet across, just above the water. At its back, where there should be raw rock, there's a flat, smooth face of old grey plaster, laid on by hand.

Back up the track, past the sheds, the warden's house stands shut with its bolt across. Its chimney gives off a last faint wisp and then nothing. In the drift, the seep trickles on in the dark. The waterline on the white wall sits a finger's width above the dark stain it was at a few minutes ago.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Sefa, secure my loose end round that oak while I keep his weight. Then fetch Hale—we need a lever, and the water’s rising.”

I keep steady tension on Pell’s rope, without hauling against his pinned leg.

“HALE! MAN DOWN! THE CART TRACK’S COLLAPSED!” I shout toward the house.

Then, down to Pell: “Rope’s staying with you. Can you see how the block’s caught your leg? Is there room beside you for someone to stand and lever it off?”

I look for a way down on the bank side, away from the broken prop and hanging case. I don’t put weight on the lip or start descending until the rope is anchored.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa turns toward the quarry, plants her feet, and lets the Lantern's little cantrip roll through her voice — not to startle, but to carry.

"Master Hale! We're at the bend — the track's given way under the outer edge! A man's gone down the old drift, pinned! I need a long timber and another rope, now!"

Then she drops the amplification, not willing to shake more stone loose, and calls down the hole: "Pell, hold quiet. Hale's house is close; I've called him back. We're not leaving you."

She glances once at the taut rope in Bram's hands and the line running down past the case. "Don't let the rope pull on him unless he slips under. The prop's holding the case; let it take its own weight a while longer. When Hale comes with a timber, we lever the block — no one climbs onto that crust."

scenes.narration:
Sefa's voice goes out over the quarry three times louder than any throat could make it. It bounces off the white faces of the cut and comes back from the terraces, and the swallows burst out of the cracks all at once. Bram's shout follows it, a caravan guard's bellow that has carried over teamsters and rain. Then Sefa lets the spell go and speaks into the hole at an ordinary pitch. A few grains of crust trickle off the lip and tick into the water. Nothing bigger falls.

Bram keeps the rope where it is. He's flat on the hard ground a body's length back from the edge, elbows dug in, and the hemp runs taut through his gloves and down past the hanging canvas bundle. He doesn't let it pull. The loose end lies coiled behind him on the track, still untied. Sefa has turned to the quarry, and he holds the full weight himself. His forearms are already feeling it.

He reads the hole while he holds it. The outer edge is the bad side. The crust there is a hand's thickness of baked chalk over rotten boards, and it's still shedding. The inner edge, on the bank side under the oak, is different. Bram can see grey drift timbers a foot under the road there, butted into solid white rock, and below them the wall drops square and dry to the water. A man coming down on a rope fixed to the oak would go down that inner wall clear of the prop and the case. He'd land in the water away from the rubble heap, close to where the old beam lies along the wall. The rope just needs to be fast to something before anyone trusts it.

Up the track the warden's bolt grates back.

Osric Hale comes out of the house at a heavy, steady jog, the gait of a man who stopped running years ago and is doing it anyway. He has a coil of rope over one shoulder, an iron pinch-bar as long as his arm in one fist and a leather bucket swinging from the other. He comes past the sheds and round the bend and stops well short of the hole, on the inner side, where he's walked for twenty years. He breathes hard through his nose and looks at it.

He doesn't ask who's down there. He looks at Bram on his belly with the rope and at the loose coil behind him. He drops the bar and the bucket, takes up the loose end and walks it to the oak. He takes two turns round the trunk below the first fork and ties it off with the same carter's knot that was on the case. He tugs it once, hard, and the oak's roots don't so much as tick.

"That'll hold him," he says to Bram. "Ease off."

Then he comes to the inner edge, stops where the timbers are, and looks down.

He looks for a long moment at the dressed white block with the sun cut into it, lying in the light at the bottom of the hole.

"Never seen that," he says. He looks along the drift into the dark, where the trickle of the seep goes on. "That's the old low drift. Runs back under toward the seam. Water's off the seam." He sets his own coil of rope down beside the bucket and the bar, at the foot of the oak. "Bar's the house's. Bucket too. Bring them back or leave them by my door."

He straightens up and looks at Sefa, then down the hole again. His jaw works once.

"Don't any of you sit in that water longer than you have to. Men get slow down the low cuts. Heavy-headed." He doesn't say anything more about it. "I'm not going down. And I go at noon. Lads are waiting."

He stays where he is for now, at the edge with his arms hanging, and doesn't go back to the house. Below him the water has crept a little higher on the white wall. The case turns slowly on Pell's silk rope, and the sun is climbing toward its height over the quiet quarry.

 (Out of game: Bram's tension on the rope, his shout and his reading of the bank-side way down were ordinary work with nothing at stake, so they were narrated without a roll.)

(Out of game: Bram's question about room to lever was put to Pell, whose player answers it in his own scene, so I haven't played the answer.)

"Master Hale! We're at the bend — the track's given way under the outer edge! A man's gone down the old drift, pinned! I need a long timber and another rope, now!"

Then she drops the amplification, not willing to shake more stone loose, and calls down the hole: "Pell, hold quiet. Hale's house is close; I've called him back. We're not leaving you."

<<<
Sefa's voice goes out over the quarry three times louder than any throat could make it. It bounces off the white faces of the cut and comes back from the terraces, and the swallows burst out of the cracks all at once. Bram's shout follows it, a caravan guard's bellow that has carried over teamsters and rain. Then Sefa lets the spell go and speaks into the hole at an ordinary pitch. A few grains of crust trickle off the lip and tick into the water. Nothing bigger falls.

Bram keeps the rope where it is. He's flat on the hard ground a body's length back from the edge, elbows dug in, and the hemp runs taut through his gloves and down past the hanging canvas bundle. He doesn't let it pull. The loose end lies coiled behind him on the track, still untied. Sefa has turned to the quarry, and he holds the full weight himself. His forearms are already feeling it.

He reads the hole while he holds it. The outer edge is the bad side. The crust there is a hand's thickness of baked chalk over rotten boards, and it's still shedding. The inner edge, on the bank side under the oak, is different. Bram can see grey drift timbers a foot under the road there, butted into solid white rock, and below them the wall drops square and dry to the water. A man coming down on a rope fixed to the oak would go down that inner wall clear of the prop and the case. He'd land in the water away from the rubble heap, close to where the old beam lies along the wall. The rope just needs to be fast to something before anyone trusts it.

Osric Hale comes out of the house at a heavy, steady jog, the gait of a man who stopped running years ago and is doing it anyway. He has a coil of rope over one shoulder, an iron pinch-bar as long as his arm in one fist and a leather bucket swinging from the other. He comes past the sheds and round the bend and stops well short of the hole, on the inner side, where he's walked for twenty years. He breathes hard through his nose and looks at it.

He doesn't ask who's down there. He looks at Bram on his belly with the rope and at the loose coil behind him. He drops the bar and the bucket, takes up the loose end and walks it to the oak. He takes two turns round the trunk below the first fork and ties it off with the same carter's knot that was on the case. He tugs it once, hard, and the oak's roots don't so much as tick.

"That'll hold him," he says to Bram. "Ease off."

Then he comes to the inner edge, stops where the timbers are, and looks down.

He looks for a long moment at the dressed white block with the sun cut into it, lying in the light at the bottom of the hole.

"Never seen that," he says. He looks along the drift into the dark, where the trickle of the seep goes on. "That's the old low drift. Runs back under toward the seam. Water's off the seam." He sets his own coil of rope down beside the bucket and the bar, at the foot of the oak. "Bar's the house's. Bucket too. Bring them back or leave them by my door."

He straightens up and looks at Sefa, then down the hole again. His jaw works once.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the rope take his weight and stops fighting the stone. He's breathing hard; he makes himself slow it.

"Right. Listen, because I've got the numbers and you don't." His voice carries up flat and even, the way he'd report a lock that won't give. "Block's far end is on cut floor, near end's on the fall. It'll lift with a lever — there's a pit-prop six feet from me, man-long. But it wants one body on the lever with a rope taking its weight and one body in the water digging, and it's an inch at a time. Two of you, it's sunset. One of you, it's never." A beat. "And the water's coming up. Finger's width since I went in. I don't get till sunset."

He twists to look at the chimney, then back up at the hole.

"Hale's still in the house — bolt's across, he doesn't walk till noon. He's got timber, he's got rope, and he's walked over these drifts twenty years. He said some of them took water; he'll know where it comes from, whether there's a sluice or a lower drift it runs off to. Sefa — go. Run, don't walk. Bang the door till he opens it. Tell him the track fell in on the bend, his carrier's pinned in a drift under it, and the water's rising. Bring him and the longest beam he's got."

To Bram: "You hold. Don't come down, don't haul, just keep me high and keep the anchor honest. If the lip goes further, tell me before it goes."

Then, grimmer: "And when Hale's here, that's two hands on the lever and the dig. Which means one of you takes the box and walks. Six hours, light to spare. Thorn gets her salt, we get paid, and nobody's sunset was wasted on me." He doesn't say who. "Decide it between you while she's running."

He takes the chunk of board, wedges it behind his back against the drift wall so he can't slide if the rope slips, keeps his free boot braced on the block, and holds still. Only his eyes move — to the waterline on the white wall, and to the smooth plaster face behind the empty socket, which has no business being there.

scenes.narration:
Pell's board grates into place behind his back against the drift wall. He stops moving and the cold takes him again, reaching right into the hip that Sefa's light had only just warmed.

His report goes up the shaft of daylight flat and even. His orders to Sefa and Bram go up after it. What comes down to him belongs to the world above, and he gets it in pieces from the bottom of the hole.

A voice rolls out across the quarry, far too loud for any throat. It comes back off the white faces, and grains of crust tick down past the case into the water by his ear. A man's shout follows it. Then there's nothing for a while but the seep somewhere off in the dark.

Then the rope under his arms changes. Before, it gave a little with every breath, the way a rope does when a man is holding it. Now it goes hard and dead, as if it had been tied off to something rooted. Footsteps come along the inner edge, slow and heavy on the hard ground. A head and shoulders block part of the light at the bank side, over the grey timbers. Grey beard, dust-white apron. Osric Hale looks down at him.

His eyes don't stay on Pell. They go to the block lying beside Pell's face with the sun cut into it, and they stay there a long time. Pell hears him say he's never seen it before. He hears him call this the old low drift, and say the water comes off the seam.

Pell has said his numbers loud enough for the warden to hear. When Osric speaks again it's to the hole, not to anyone up top.

"Heard you. Two's right." He says it without any feeling, the way he'd confirm a load count. "No sluice. Never was one down here. That water comes in off the seam and it doesn't go out. It fills to its level and sits."

His jaw works once.

"Not me on the lever. I don't go down the low cuts. Not for you, not for anybody." He doesn't give a reason. "I go at noon."

He doesn't move away from the edge, either. He stays crouched at the inner lip with his forearms on his knees. Down in the drift his shadow lies across the water, and the pink dust drifts slowly through it.

Pell lies still and lets his eyes do the work. The waterline on the white wall hasn't visibly moved since he last looked, but the dark stain it left a few minutes ago is now a finger's width under the surface, and the wall above it is wet. The water around his chest has settled from milky to merely cloudy. Here, close to the surface, it smells faintly of something. It isn't the flat chalk smell of the drift. It's sweeter than that, almost like flour.

Then there's the plaster. The square socket the block tore out of sits a hand's width above the water, two feet across. The smooth grey face at the back of it isn't quite flat to the rock. The block took a sliver of plaster with it at one corner as it came away, and behind the broken edge there's a thin black gap, no wider than a knife blade. There's no white stone in it, just dark. When the seep goes quiet for a moment, he can hear the trickle again, from somewhere he can't place.

Overhead the sun is still climbing. Its patch of light on the water has crept a few inches along the drift since he fell.
