messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps to the oak, keeping off the bad lip. "Bram, you're the one who can get down there — but not in mail. Leave the shield and the hauberk here; the water's too close to risk their weight. Take Hale's bar and put the rope under your arms, tied off at the oak. I'll watch the lip and feed you enough rope to reach the old drift floor."

She touches Bram's shoulder as he readies, and the air warms with a thin, steady glow, like a lamp behind glass. "Lantern, steady his hands."

To Osric, without turning: "Stay until noon if you can. I won't ask you down, Master Hale — only for your eye on the road and the rope."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I ease Pell’s weight onto the anchored rope and get up on the bank side.

“I’ll take the bar down. Hale, help Sefa work the ropes from solid ground. If I go dull or stop answering, haul me out.”

I secure Hale’s rope to the oak, leaving enough length to tie a loop snugly around my torso as a lifeline. I leave my pack and weapons beside my shield.

“Sefa, lower the bar once I’m down. When Pell’s free, take up his rope—steady, not a jerk.”

I descend along the sound inner wall using the anchored rope, clear of the case and rotten prop, aiming for the old beam if it offers firm footing.

“Pell, tell me where it’s pressing. I’m coming beside you.”

Once down, I intend to use the pinch-bar with a firm fulcrum to lift the block just enough for Pell to withdraw his leg, keeping our hands out from underneath it.

She would watch the lip and feed you rope down to the old drift floor. She put a hand on your shoulder, and a thin, steady glow came up under her palm, warm as a lamp behind glass, and soaked into the rings of your mail. "Lantern, steady his hands," she said. Without turning, she told Osric Hale she wouldn't ask him down, only for his eye on the road and the rope, and asked him to stay until noon if he could. Osric didn't turn round either. "Said noon."

You lowered your end of Pell's rope until the oak took the full weight, then got up off your belly on the inner side. Your pack, longsword and javelins went down on the hard white ground beside the shield. You kept your chain mail on. You took Osric's coil from the foot of the oak, made it fast round the trunk below your own knot, and tied the other end in a snug loop round your chest under the arms.

"If I go dull or stop answering, haul me out," you said.

Osric looked at the loop, then at the hole, and took the slack of the lifeline in both fists. "Keep talking, then. I'll hear it stop."

You went over the inner edge with the rope in your gloves and your boots on the grey drift timbers. Below them the wall was sound, dry and square, just as it had looked from above. You walked yourself down it hand over hand, with the case turning on its silk rope off to your right, well clear. The cold hit you at the waist like a blow. Then your boots found the cut floor, and you stood with the water halfway up your ribs and the mail dragging at your shoulders. Down here the drift smells of wet chalk, and under that of something sweeter, close to the surface, like a flour bin left open. The old pit-prop lay along the wall about where it was said to be, a man's length of grey timber, half under the water.

Up top, Osric crouched at the inner lip with the lifeline wrapped once round his forearm. He reached the iron pinch-bar down at arm's length, holding the end. You took it out of the air above your head.

You waded to the near end of the block, where the white stone sits on the slumped heap of fall. You felt under the water for something hard to rest the bar on. The paste wouldn't do. Beside the heap you found a squared chunk of the road's crust, knocked the soft off it and bedded it on the cut floor, against the edge of the rubble. Then you set the bar's tip under the near corner of the block, laid the shaft across the chunk, and leaned your whole weight into it.

He walks himself down it hand over hand, with the case turning on its silk rope off to his right, well clear. The cold hits him at the waist like a blow. Then his boots find the cut floor, and he stands with the water halfway up his ribs and the mail dragging at his shoulders. Down here the drift smells of wet chalk, and under that of something sweeter, close to the surface, like a flour bin left open. The old pit-prop lies along the wall about where it was said to be, a man's length of grey timber, half under the water.

Up top, Osric crouches at the inner lip with the lifeline wrapped once round his forearm. He reaches the iron pinch-bar down at arm's length, holding the end. Bram takes it out of the air above his head.

Bram wades to the near end of the block, where the white stone sits on the slumped heap of fall. He feels under the water for something hard to rest the bar on. The paste won't do. Beside the heap he finds a squared chunk of the road's crust, knocks the soft off it and beds it on the cut floor, against the edge of the rubble. Then he sets the bar's tip under the near corner of the block, lays the shaft across the chunk, and leans his whole weight into it.

The bar bows. The chunk of crust grinds into the cut floor and holds. For a long moment nothing moves but the water round Bram's chest. Then the near corner of the block comes up off the heap with a sucking sound, a slow inch of white stone rising out of the milky water, and stays there as long as Bram keeps his weight on the iron. The lift has worked. Whatever has been bearing down on the leg beneath, the block isn't doing it now.

Bram can feel at once what the lift hasn't done. As the stone rises, the paste under it moves too. Grey chalk mud slumps in from every side to fill the gap, and it fills it nearly as fast as the corner comes up. The leg is still down in that heap, bedded in it. Between the block's underside and the top of the rubble there's an open space now, about as wide as two fingers, and it would take a flat stone or a wedge of board pushed in. Bram's hands are both on the bar, and his weight is all on it. There's no hand left over to put anything into that gap. The iron is already hot in his gloves. The old miners' rule says a man can hold a lift like this for about a hundred count before his shoulders start to tell him otherwise, and Bram's say it now.

Up at the inner lip, Osric hasn't moved. He's crouched with the lifeline once round his forearm and his eyes on the water round Bram, not on the block. Sefa stands by the oak with the slack of Pell's rope and Bram's lifeline both within reach, and the warmth of her blessing has gone out of Bram's shoulder now it's been used.

The seep trickles on along the drift in the dark. The sun's patch of light has moved a hand's width farther along the water, and it isn't midday yet.

 Sefa's blessing did its part, but only a small one. When Bram leaned into the bar, the Lantern's warmth gave his grip a little more steadiness, enough to keep the iron from skidding on the crust and no more. The rest of that inch came from Bram's own back.

You took Osric's coil from the foot of the oak, made it fast round the trunk below your own knot, and tied the other end in a snug loop round your chest under the arms.

"If I go dull or stop answering, haul me out," you said.

Osric looked at the loop, then at the hole, and took the slack of the lifeline in both fists. "Keep talking, then. I'll hear it stop."

You went over the inner edge with the rope in your gloves and your boots on the grey drift timbers. Below them the wall was sound, dry and square, just as it had looked from above. You walked yourself down it hand over hand, with the case turning on its silk rope off to your right, well clear. The cold hit you at the waist like a blow. Then your boots found the cut floor, and you stood with the water halfway up your ribs and the mail dragging at your shoulders. Down here the drift smells of wet chalk, and under that of something sweeter, close to the surface, like a flour bin left open. The old pit-prop lay along the wall about where it was said to be, a man's length of grey timber, half under the water.

Up top, Osric crouched at the inner lip with the lifeline wrapped once round his forearm. He reached the iron pinch-bar down at arm's length, holding the end. You took it out of the air above your head.

You waded to the near end of the block, where the white stone sits on the slumped heap of fall. You felt under the water for something hard to rest the bar on. The paste wouldn't do. Beside the heap you found a squared chunk of the road's crust, knocked the soft off it and bedded it on the cut floor, against the edge of the rubble. Then you set the bar's tip under the near corner of the block, laid the shaft across the chunk, and leaned your whole weight into it.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell feels it before he hears anything — the vice on his shin eases by a hair, the block's weight going up off him into something creaking above the water. He doesn't wait to be told, and he doesn't ask how.

"It's up — *hold it there, Bram, don't breathe.*" He gets both hands under the water, down along his own calf, and claws the paste out from under it in fast double handfuls, not digging the block out any more, just making room for the leg. Then he pulls — knee bent, foot pointed, leg sliding back toward him along the floor the way you draw a blade out of a sheath, away from the near end where the block will drop. Slow, steady, no kicking. If it hangs up on the shin, he turns the foot and tries again; he's wriggled through tighter spaces than a gap under a stone.

The moment the foot clears, he hauls himself hand over hand up the dead rope a yard and gets his good knee on the fallen board, out of the block's reach. "Clear! Let it down, let it down easy."

Only then, hanging there, dripping, with the knee screaming, does he look up at Hale.

"Not for anybody." He says it back without heat. "Twenty years here and you've never seen the block that was mortared into the wall of your own drift, and you won't come down the low cuts, and the water smells like a baker's shop." He wipes his face. "I'm not asking. I'm climbing out of your hole and walking your box to Beregost. But when I carry your letter to Thorn, I'll have been in this drift, and she'll ask me what it was like. Tell me what to say about that." He tips his head at the plaster face with the knife-thin black gap behind it. "Or don't, and I'll tell her what I saw."

Then, up to Bram and Sefa: "Rope. I'm coming up the far wall, away from the broken lip. Case after me, on its own line — nobody leans out for it. And the knee's gone, so the long walk's going to be slower than I promised."

scenes.narration:
The weight comes up off his shin. It's only an inch and it creaks the whole way, but Pell feels it leave the bone.

His warning goes up to Bram, and then his hands are under the water. The paste behaves differently now. With the block held off it, nothing presses it back into the gap after each handful. It still slumps, but slowly, and his double handfuls are faster than it is. He scoops it out from under the calf two handfuls at a time, again and again, and the water around his chest turns thick and white. The calf comes up off the heap. He draws the leg back the way he meant to, knee bent, foot pointed, slow and steady, and it comes. It slides a hand's width along the floor toward him, away from the near end of the block.

Then it stops.

The calf is clear. The foot isn't. Below the ankle his leg runs on under the middle of the block, and there the lift is almost nothing. The bar raises the near corner and the block pivots on its far end, where it sits on cut floor, so halfway along it has come up half an inch at most. Under there, a slab of road crust that came down with the fall has jammed across his instep and pins the foot in the rubble. He turns the foot one way and his ankle bone grinds against the edge of the slab and stays put. He turns it the other way and gets the same. The boot isn't snagged on anything. The foot itself is pressed flat into the heap under the crust, and the wrenched knee makes him feel every try.

His fingers follow the leg down as far as they'll go. They find his ankle, the top of the boot and the near edge of the crust slab, and nothing past that. Lying where he is with the block across him, he can't reach past its side. The slab's far edge and the rubble under his instep are on the other side of the block. Someone would have to kneel in the water over there to get at them, with both hands free and nothing on top of him.

There's grit in the paste he pulled out. The grains are hard and sharp-edged, the same pale pink as the dust in the crease of Thorn's case, and they run all through the chalk mud he dug from under his leg. The sweet smell rises thicker off the stirred water, like flour and warm sugar. Halfway through it a yawn takes him, wide enough to crack his jaw.

Above him the bar creaks. The block stays where it is, its near corner an inch up out of the milky water, held there by the weight on the iron.

Osric is still crouched at the inner lip with his forearms on his knees and the lifeline wrapped once round his wrist. He watched the leg come back a hand's width and stop, and he says nothing. His eyes move from the water at Pell's chest to Pell's face and stay there a moment longer than before.

Somewhere off in the dark the seep keeps trickling. The patch of sunlight on the water has crept across to the edge of the sunburst block and lies on the cut rays. On the white wall the wet line sits a hair higher than it did a quarter of an hour ago.

 A note on each of Pell's four actions from that turn:

1. **Digging the paste out from under his calf:** no roll. With Bram's lever holding the block off, it was simple handwork, and his calf came up clear of the heap.
2. **Drawing the leg back and turning the foot:** no roll, because the turn already settled it. The lever only raises the middle of the block about half an inch. A slab of road crust there pins his foot across the instep, so no die could free it this round. The leg came back about a hand's width and then stopped.
3. **Climbing the rope and calling "Clear!":** this couldn't happen. Pell planned it for after his foot came free, and it didn't come free.
4. **Speaking to Hale:** I didn't play this. Pell planned it for after he was out and on the rope, so it's still his to say next round if he wants to, as written or changed.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Stone’s up, Pell. Mud’s still holding you. Work your leg loose gently—I’ve got the weight.”

I keep both hands on the bar and hold steady.

“Hale! Need a flat wedge in this gap, two fingers thick. Sound wood or stone. Can you pass one to Pell? Don’t touch the fulcrum.”

“Sefa, take up Pell’s slack as he frees himself. Easy tension, not a hard haul.”

I keep talking so Hale can hear I’m alert. “Still steady. But we’ve less than a hundred count. Pell, can you reach the gap to chock it?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa moves as close as she dares to the inner lip, one hand on the oak. "Hold the bar where it is, Bram — don't ease it. I'll put something under the corner from here."

She lets go of the trunk only long enough to work the air. A spectral hand shimmers into being above the rubble near the edge, pale as chalk dust. She sends it down among the scattered stones until it closes on a flat, palm-sized piece of the road-crust — not too heavy, not too thick — and carries it down the wall toward the open gap under the block.

"Coming in now, near the corner," she calls, guiding the hand with small, deliberate movements while her other hand stays braced on the oak. "If it starts to slip, say so."

cards.title: Mage Hand: setting a chock of crust under the block's near corner in murky water (Dexterity +2)

presses.text:
The spectral hand carries the flat cake of road crust down past the timbers and over Bram's shoulder, then in under the lifted corner of the block. For a moment the milky water hides it, and you work by the feel of the unseen magic alone — then the crust seats itself against the rubble with a small, gritty bite, and the corner of the block comes down onto it and holds.

Bram gives a short, breathless word of thanks from below, and eases off the bar just enough to prove the chock isn't going to spit out. The block stays. His weight comes off the iron by slow degrees, and still it stays.

"Good," he calls up. "That's good. Pell, it's off your foot — go slow, don't stir the paste more than you must."

The water below churns white as Pell begins to shift, but the mage hand has done its work. You stay braced at the oak, one hand on the trunk, the slack of Pell's rope easy in the other. Through the drifting dust and the lapping of the water, the old drift still runs away into the dark, and the sun's light has crept another inch along the wall.
presses.reply:
Thanks. The image of Sefa working blind by the feel of the hand is a good one, and it fits her. Here is how I'll take it.

**These stand as written, because they are Sefa's:** she sends the spectral hand down past the timbers and over Bram's shoulder with the flat cake of crust, and tries to seat it under the lifted near corner. She stays braced at the oak, one hand on the trunk, with the slack of Pell's rope easy in the other.

**These are suggestions, and the die and the world decide them:**
- **Whether the chock seats and holds.** That is exactly what the waiting card decides. When you press [Onward], the narration tells it as an event, either way. If it holds, I'll describe it holding. If it doesn't, the crust goes somewhere in that milky water and the block stays on Bram's back.
- **What a chock under the near corner does for Pell.** Pell's scene has its own state, already narrated to his player, and I'll keep to it. A good chock does what a chock does and no more. It won't change anything it can't reach. So read "it's off your foot" as a hope, not a fact.
- **Bram's thanks, his easing off the bar and his call down to Pell.** Those belong to Bram's player, to say and do in his own round if he wants to. The same goes for Pell shifting in the water; that's his player's.
- **The drift and the light.** The water, the dark of the drift and the sun on the wall are mine to describe as they stand.

One small rules note: the card is fair as called. Mage Hand can lift that crust easily, since the weight is well inside what it can carry and Bram is within its reach. Setting it blind, under murky water and into a two-finger gap, is the uncertain part, so it stays a Dexterity check against DC 10.

scenes.narration:
Bram's voice comes up out of the hole steady and a little tight. He's breathing through his teeth with all his weight on the iron.

At the inner lip Sefa keeps one hand on the oak. With the other she draws a shape in the air, and a hand forms above the scattered rubble at the edge of the track. It's pale and see-through, the colour of chalk dust. It drifts across the stones, closes on a flat cake of road crust about the size of a palm and as thick as two fingers, and carries it down past the grey timbers. It goes over Bram's shoulder and down to the block, where the near corner stands an inch out of the milky water.

Osric watches the hand go by a yard from his face. He doesn't flinch, but his grip on Bram's lifeline shifts once.

The gap is half under the water. The paste is slumping in at its edges, and Sefa can't see the bottom of it from up here.

Sefa moves the hand in small, careful jerks. She feels her way more than sees it, the way someone threads a needle in a bad light. The crust cake touches the block's underside, slides along it, and finds the gap. She pushes, and the hand drives it in edge-first under the near corner until it's bedded on the rubble with its flat face up against the white stone. A little paste squeezes out round it and clouds the water. The chock stays where it is. Sefa lets the hand open and it fades out in the air above the water.

Bram feels the iron change in his hands before anyone says anything. He lets the bar up a finger's width, then another. The block comes down with it a hair and stops on the crust with a small gritty crunch. It doesn't move after that. He gives it a full breath, then lifts his weight off the bar altogether. The near corner stays where the bar had it, an inch out of the water, sitting on Sefa's chock. His shoulders burn as the strain goes out of them. For the first time since he came down the wall, both his hands are free.

Up at the lip, Osric hasn't let go of the lifeline. With his free hand he reaches over to the inner edge and pulls loose a split length of old drift timber about a forearm long. It's grey and dry and still sound when he knocks it on the rock. He lays it on the timbers at the lip, where a hand reaching up from below could take it.

"Board," he says. "Sound. There's more in the edge if you want it." He doesn't say anything else, and he doesn't come any closer to the hole than the timbers.

The chock can only do one thing, and Bram can feel that too. It holds the near corner. Down the middle of the block the stone still lies almost as low as before, across the slab of road crust under the water, and that end isn't his to reach from where he's standing. The slab's far edge is on the other side of the block. The old pit-prop lies along the wall over there, half under the water, a man's length of grey timber.

The cold has worked into Bram's ribs through the mail. There's something else as well, lighter than the cold: a warm heaviness behind his eyes, like the end of a long night watch when the fire's been good. It comes up off the water with that sweet smell of an open flour bin, and it goes when he blinks.

The seep keeps trickling in the dark of the drift. Up on the road the sun is climbing toward midday over the white faces of the cut. Pell's canvas bundle still hangs on its silk rope from the broken prop, turning slowly.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops trying to turn the foot. He's learned the shape of the trap now; grinding the ankle on the slab just spends what he's got.

The yawn frightens him more than the water does. He shakes it off, lifts his chin, and breathes through his nose up toward the daylight rather than the stirred milk around his chest.

"Hold the lift, Bram. Don't lower it, don't lift more — just hold. Calf's out. Foot's jammed under a slab of crust on the *far* side of the block, past where I can reach. Someone has to kneel in the water over there and dig it off my instep. That's hands, not strength." A beat. "Sefa. You're lighter than him and he's on the bar. Far wall, away from the broken lip, on your own line. Hale — you've got my rope. Don't let it off your wrist till I'm up. After that you go where you like."

Then, lower, so it carries to Sefa but not as a shout: "And listen before you come. The grit under my leg is the same pink as what's in Thorn's case, and the water's gone sweet with it — flour and sugar. I've been breathing it a quarter-hour and I just yawned fit to break my jaw. I don't think that's dye-salt. Keep your face out of the water, don't drink it, don't lick your fingers, and work fast. If I go quiet, slap me."

He gets the fallen board wedged tighter at his back, winds a turn of the lifeline round his own forearm so he can't slip under if his head nods, and sets his free hand on the block's upper face, right over the cut sun, to feel the moment it shifts.

To Hale, flat, not looking away from the plaster face and its knife-thin black gap: "Twenty years you've counted loads out of here. Loads of what, Master Hale?"

Pell stops turning the foot. He lifts his chin to the light and breathes through his nose, and the yawn drains out of his jaw slowly.

While he's calling up to Bram, the drift changes around him. The creak of the iron stops. Something pale and see-through went past over the water a moment ago, a hand the colour of chalk dust carrying a flat cake of crust, and now it's gone. Under the near corner of the block there's a small gritty crunch. Then nothing. When Pell sets his palm flat on the cut sun, the stone is cold and dead still. It isn't trembling the way a held lift does. It's sitting on something.

He works the fallen board tighter behind his back and takes a turn of the rope loop round his forearm. The hemp is wet and rough. If his head nods now, his own arm holds him up. His foot is still pinned flat across the instep under the middle of the block, exactly as before.

Under his hand, the black gap behind the plaster is a finger's length from his knuckles. There's air in it. It's barely there, a breath on wet skin, colder than the drift. It carries the same sweetness, flour and sugar, a little stronger than off the water.

At the inner lip Osric hasn't moved. Pell's orders go past him, and the warning about the grit and the yawning. His eyes are on Pell's face, and they stay there.

"Yours is on the oak," he says. "I've his." He moves his wrist an inch so Pell can see the hemp wound round it, and it isn't Pell's rope. "Oak won't let go."

Then Pell's question reaches him. He looks along the drift into the dark before he answers, the way he looked at the cart this morning.

"Stone. White stone, cut and squared. Beregost had it, and the Gate when the Gate paid. Lime, when the kilns still ran." A pause. "Salt. A case a season, off the low walls, when an order came. Men picked it by hand. Short shifts."

That's all he gives. Then, because Pell yawned, he adds more than he was asked.

"Short, because they got slow. I said. Heavy-headed." His jaw works. "Don't sleep down there."

He says nothing else. He stays crouched with the lifeline round his wrist. His shadow lies over the water by the sunburst, and the pink dust turns slowly through it.

The seep trickles in the dark. The patch of sun has moved off the cut rays onto the plaster below the socket. The waterline on the white wall sits where it was, and the wall above it is still wet.

 None of these four needed a roll. Each was a decision or a spoken line, with nothing uncertain to settle:

1. **Holding still:** Pell stops turning the foot and holds still. That was his own choice, so it simply happened as written.
2. **"Hold the lift":** Pell said it, and Bram heard it. The block had already settled onto Sefa's chock before the words reached him. What Bram does now is his player's call.
3. **Sending Sefa to the far wall:** Pell said it, and Sefa heard it. Whether she climbs down, and how, is up to Sefa's player in her own scene.
4. **The rope:** Pell didn't hand Hale anything. He only told Hale to keep hold of "my rope." Osric answered that Pell's rope is tied to the oak and that the rope round his own wrist is Bram's lifeline. Pell's loop is still anchored to the oak and holding.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell stops trying to turn the foot. He's learned the shape of the trap now; grinding the ankle on the slab just spends what he's got.

The yawn frightens him more than the water does. He shakes it off, lifts his chin, and breathes through his nose up toward the daylight rather than the stirred milk around his chest.

"Hold the lift, Bram. Don't lower it, don't lift more — just hold. Calf's out. Foot's jammed under a slab of crust on the *far* side of the block, past where I can reach. Someone has to kneel in the water over there and dig it off my instep. That's hands, not strength." A beat. "Sefa. You're lighter than him and he's on the bar. Far wall, away from the broken lip, on your own line. Hale — you've got my rope. Don't let it off your wrist till I'm up. After that you go where you like."

Then, lower, so it carries to Sefa but not as a shout: "And listen before you come. The grit under my leg is the same pink as what's in Thorn's case, and the water's gone sweet with it — flour and sugar. I've been breathing it a quarter-hour and I just yawned fit to break my jaw. I don't think that's dye-salt. Keep your face out of the water, don't drink it, don't lick your fingers, and work fast. If I go quiet, slap me."

He gets the fallen board wedged tighter at his back, winds a turn of the lifeline round his own forearm so he can't slip under if his head nods, and sets his free hand on the block's upper face, right over the cut sun, to feel the moment it shifts.

To Hale, flat, not looking away from the plaster face and its knife-thin black gap: "Twenty years you've counted loads out of here. Loads of what, Master Hale?"
>>>

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps both ropes in view — Pell's weight still on the oak, Bram's lifeline in Osric's grip — and calls down, "The chock's under the near corner only, Bram. If you lift the middle, don't trust it alone. There's another length of sound board at the lip, and the pit-prop lies along the far wall below you."

She pulls in a slow breath and lets the Lantern's smallest blessing run up her wrist, not into her own hands this time, but down the air to Bram, a faint light settling on his arms like the pause before a toll.

"Guidance on you," she says. "For whatever you lift next."

Then, to Osric, quieter: "If the road gives way any further, haul Bram out and don't wait for my word."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Getting heavy behind the eyes, Hale. Still thinking clear, but we need out soon.”

I take the sound board from the lip and keep the pinch-bar with me.

“Pell, where’s it still catching you? Point me to it.”

Keeping my lifeline clear, I move along the sound wall toward the far side, testing the floor before each step. I want to reach the remaining pressure point without disturbing Sefa’s chock or the prop holding the case.

If I can get firm footing there, I set the bar on a solid support to lift that side, with Hale’s board ready for Pell or Sefa’s hand to wedge into the gap.

“Sefa, be ready to chock this side. Then we draw him clear while both sides are held.”

screens.Bram Halloway:
From above, Sefa calls down that the chock sits only under the near corner, so if you lift the middle you shouldn't trust it alone. She adds that a second sound board waits at the lip and that the pit-prop is on the floor along the far wall below you. Then she draws a slow breath and lets the Lantern's smallest blessing run off her wrist. It drifts down the shaft of daylight, past the turning canvas bundle, and settles on your forearms as a faint warmth under the cold, waiting for the next thing you put your strength to. She names it guidance, meant for whatever you lift next. Then, more quietly, she tells Osric to haul you out without waiting for her word if the road gives way any further. Osric doesn't look round. He says he wasn't going to.

You say your head is getting heavy behind the eyes, though you're still thinking clear, and that you need out soon. Osric answers at once. The lads did an hour at the low walls, he says, and then went up into the air, or they didn't come up right. You've had a quarter of that. He says nothing after.

You reach up past the grey drift timbers and take Osric's board off the lip. It is a forearm of split, dry wood, and it sounds true when you knock it. You keep the pinch-bar in your other fist. You ask Pell where it's catching him. The answer had already come up out of the water a moment earlier, when Pell called it to the top: the foot is under a slab of road crust on the far side of the block, past where Pell can reach.

So you go to the far side. You keep your back to the sound wall and the lifeline clear of the prop. You wade round the block's far end, where its white weight rests square on the level floor the old miners cut. The water drags at your mail with every step, and you test each one with your boot before you trust it. The floor here is firm stone, and the fall never reached it. Past the block's far end the old pit-prop lies along the wall, grey and half-sunk, and beyond it the drift runs back into the dark. The sweet smell is stronger on this side. It isn't by much, but you notice it. It's thicker away from the light and the hole, the way a bakehouse smells stronger the closer you get to the oven door.

You can't see the slab. The water is milk here too, stirred up from Pell's digging. You find the slab with your boot and then with one hand, reaching down along the block's long far edge. Along this stretch the block's underside doesn't sit on the floor. It sits on the heap of the fall, and in the heap is a flat edge of baked crust as wide as your palm, jammed under the stone. That's the slab. Its far edge is right here under your fingers, bedded in rubble and paste.

You can't push the bar's tip under the stone where the far end sits flat on cut floor. Where it sits on the rubble you can. You work your fingers in beside the slab and claw out a pocket of paste. You knock a seat into the heap with the bar's tip and find a fist-sized lump of hard chalk on the cut floor to bed the shaft across. You lay Osric's board flat on top of the block over the cut sun, where a hand from either side could take it. Then you set the tip, set your feet, and feel the warmth of Sefa's blessing gather in your forearms as you lean into the iron.

Her warning goes down the hole, the near-corner chock, the board at the lip, the pit-prop along the far wall. Then she breathes slowly and lets the smallest of the Lantern's blessings run off her wrist. It drifts down through the shaft of daylight, past the turning canvas bundle, and settles on Bram's forearms as a faint warmth under the cold, waiting for the next thing he puts his strength to.

"Guidance on you. For whatever you lift next."

Then, more quietly, to Osric: "If the road gives way any further, haul Bram out and don't wait for my word."

Osric doesn't look round. "Wasn't going to."

From the bottom of the hole Bram's voice comes up steady, with the edge of the cold in it. "Getting heavy behind the eyes, Hale. Still thinking clear, but we need out soon."

This time Osric does answer straight away. "Lads did an hour at the low walls. Then up into the air, or they didn't come up right." He shifts the lifeline on his wrist. "You've had a quarter of it."

He wades round the block's far end, where its white weight rests square on the level floor the old miners cut. The water drags at his mail every step. He tests each step with his boot before he trusts it. The floor here is firm stone, and the fall never reached it. Past the block's far end the old pit-prop lies along the wall, grey and half-sunk, and beyond it the drift runs back into the dark. The sweet smell is stronger on this side. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
The chocked stone under his palm tells him before anyone says it: the bar's free. He puts that together with the pale hand he saw carrying crust.

"Sefa — that hand. The one that set the chock." He keeps his voice level, pitched up the shaft. "It's got no face to keep out of the water and no lungs to breathe this sweetness with. Send it round the far side of the block, under the surface, and get its fingers under the slab on my instep. A hand's all it is and a hand's all I need. Lift the slab toward you, away from me, and I'll pull the foot the second it eases."

While she works it, he does what he can from his side. His arm won't reach past the block — but his shortsword's two feet longer than his arm. He draws it slow under the water, turns it flat, and feeds the blade along his own shin, past the ankle, under the block's middle where the gap is half an inch, hunting for the slab's near edge with the point the way he'd hunt a lock's last pin with a pick. Lockpick's patience, not a labourer's shove: find the edge, set the point, then lever it a hair upward and outward with the guard braced against the block's underside.

"Bram — you're off the bar. Stay up. If that chock goes, I want you on the iron again before the block's down, not after. And somebody keep talking to me." He grinds the wrenched knee against the board on purpose, lets the pain cut through the sweet fog, and does *not* look at the gap behind the plaster, because he can feel it breathing on his knuckles and that's the sort of thing that can wait for daylight and a dry pair of boots.

To Hale, without turning his head: "Heavy-headed. Short shifts. And a case a season to a Gate house that stopped paying you the same week it bought this one." Flat. "I'll put that in my own words to Thorn. You'll want to be there."

cards.title: Sleight of Hand: work the shortsword blind under the block and lever the crust slab off his instep

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Sefa isn't here to answer, and the hand you asked for doesn't come. What reaches you is what you do yourself and what Bram does.

Bram never stayed up on the bar as you told him to. He has waded round to the far side of the block, got the iron under the far edge and put all his weight on it. You hear his breath hiss through his teeth. The block gives a deep, sucking groan. Under your palm the cut sun moves. The whole stone tilts on the crust cake under the near corner and rises through the middle, and iron creaks from beyond it, close to the water.

Your instep feels it first. The weight of the crust slab goes. Only the cold and the mud packed round your foot hold it now, not stone.

You draw the shortsword under the water slowly, so the stirred chalk won't swirl, turn it flat and feed it down along your shin. The water is too thick to see through, so you go by feel. The point slides past your ankle into the gap under the block's middle. With Bram on the bar the gap is wider than it was. You feel for the slab's near edge the way you'd feel for the last pin in a lock.

places.Pell Dunmore: in the water by the tilted block, foot trapped under the slab

presses.text:
The point finds the slab's edge like a pick finding its pin — a tiny catch, then a seat. Pell doesn't shove. He braces the guard against the block's underside, rolls his wrist a quarter-turn, and the crust lifts off his instep with a wet, grating sigh. The mud lets go of the boot a heartbeat later.

He pulls the leg the way he's been waiting to for half an hour: knee bent, foot pointed, straight back along the floor toward himself. It comes. All of it.

"*Clear.* Foot's out, Bram — let it down, easy, on your count, and get your own feet out from under it." He drags the shortsword back along his shin, slow, so it doesn't catch anything on the way, and sheathes it wet. Then he hauls hand over hand up the oak-anchored rope until he's clear of the block's fall-line, gets his good knee on the wedged board, and hangs there a moment with his forehead against the chalk wall, breathing daylight through his nose.

When the block's down and the water's done sloshing, he looks for Bram across it.

"You were meant to stay up." It's not a complaint. "Thank you. Now get out of this water before you start yawning too. Far wall, away from the broken lip — I'll be behind you on the line. The knee's not taking weight, so I'll be climbing on my arms; Second-Story Work says I can, and today it had better be right."

He gets a hand on the lifeline, tests it, and starts up the far wall — chimney-style, back and good foot and both hands, a yard at a time. Halfway, he pauses just long enough to hook two fingers under the silk rope where it still hangs from the prop, and tug once. The case swings and holds. Dry.

"Hale. When I'm up, you cut the box free and lower it on *this* line to whoever's below the hole — nobody leans. Then I want a strip of your apron for the knee and a straight piece of timber to lean on, and we'll both be at the Burning Wizard before Thorn is."

He doesn't look at the gap behind the plaster on the way past. He can still feel it breathing cold and sweet on his wet knuckles, and he's filing it where he files all the things that will still be there tomorrow.

- Everything he says to Bram and to Hale, as written.
- How he plans to climb: on his arms, chimney-style up the far wall on the line, then a pause to hook the silk rope and give it one tug.

scenes.narration:
Under Pell's palm the cut sun moves.

The chock has been dead still for a minute, but now the far side of the block gives a deep sucking groan. The whole stone tilts on the crust cake under the near corner, slowly, and rises through the middle. Iron creaks from beyond it, close to the water, and Bram's breathing comes through his teeth. Bram isn't up. He's waded round and is down on the far side with the bar under the far edge and all his weight on it. Pell's instep feels it first. The crust slab's weight goes, and now it's only the cold and the mud packed round his foot holding it, not stone.

Pell has called for the hand, but the hand isn't his to bring. What he can do himself is the blade. He draws the shortsword under the water slowly, so the stirred chalk won't swirl, turns it flat and feeds it down along his own shin. The water's too thick to see through, so he goes by feel. The point slides past the ankle and into the gap under the block's middle, which is wider now with Bram on the bar. He feels for the slab's near edge the way he'd feel for the last pin in a lock.

The point finds the edge.

It's no wider than a palm. The edge is a lip of baked crust lying across the top of his boot, slick with paste, and on the first pass the blade skids off it. Pell doesn't push. He backs the point off a hair, tilts it, and feels for the place where the crust meets the rubble under it, the seam where it's weakest. He finds it and sets the point there. He braces the guard against the underside of the block, which Bram is holding up, and makes the sword a lever an inch long. Then he lifts.

The slab comes up off his instep slowly, a hair and then a finger's width, sucking free of the mud. He keeps the blade turning, upward and outward, the way you turn a wrench in a stiff lock once the pins are set. The slab tips. It slides off the top of his foot and away from him, down the far side of the heap, and comes to rest somewhere near Bram's boots with a dull grind he hears through the water.

Pell pulls. The foot comes, and this time it keeps coming. The ankle slides back along the floor past the middle of the block, past the line where the stone was lying on it, and out into open water on his side. For the first time since the road went, nothing of the block is over any part of his leg. If the bar slipped now and the stone came down, it would come down on mud.

Then the heel stops, as if a hand had closed on it.

He keeps the sword in his fist and follows the boot down with the point, carefully, because it's his own ankle in there. Running along the drift floor under him is a groove: a straight, square gutter cut into the floor rock, a hand wide and a hand deep, the kind old miners cut to lead water away. The fall drove his heel down into it. The block's weight and the slab's weight then packed the gutter round it for an hour with crust, splinters and chalk paste, so tight it has set like lime-mortar. The point taps on it and only chips. It isn't the kind of thing you lift. Somebody has to dig it out with a narrow point, a crumb at a time, by feel or with the water bailed down, and keep away from the ankle bone. The sword is too long and too sharp to use in there blind. A dagger would do it, or the bar's tip, or a hand with no flesh to cut.

Up at the inner lip, Osric has heard every word Pell said to him. He keeps his eyes on the water round Bram.

"Your words." A pause. "I'll be with the lads."

Pell asked for someone to talk to him, and Osric doesn't chat. But a moment later he starts counting in the same flat voice he'd use for loads coming off the face, low and steady, down into the hole. He's counting Bram's hold on the iron.

"Fifteen. Twenty. Twenty-five."

His fists don't move on the lifeline. Pell grinds his wrenched knee into the board on purpose, and the hot jab cuts through the sweet heaviness behind his eyes for a few breaths. Then the heaviness comes back, a little slower each time. Close to his knuckles the black gap behind the plaster keeps breathing its faint cold sugar onto his wet skin, and he doesn't look at it.

"Thirty. Thirty-five."

The patch of sun lies on the water past the block's far end. On the white wall the wet line hasn't moved.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Up! Sefa—the board on top. Get it into this gap with your hand spell, now. Arms won’t last.”

I hold my weight on the bar, keeping the lift steady.

“Pell, stone’s off the slab. Work your foot clear while we’ve got it. Tell us the instant you’re free.”

I keep my eyes on the gap and call up to Hale, “Still awake. Once he’s loose, get him up first. Then me.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps a half-pace along the inner edge, keeping clear of the bad lip, and calls down, "Hold it, Bram. Five more heartbeats at the iron, and I'll have the board under the far edge."

She lets go of the oak only with her spell-hand, and the spectral hand kindles again above the hole, pale as dusted glass. It drops to the block, closes on Osric's board where it lies over the cut sun, and lifts it.

Carrying the board low along the block's face, she guides it past the rising far edge and under it into the widening gap. "Coming in on your far side," she says, her voice steady though the heat of the sun is on her neck. "Pell, when I say so, work your leg free slowly — not before."

She holds the hand there, feeling for the moment the board takes the weight from the iron.

presses.text:
The mage hand slides the pointed end of Osric's board along the face of the tilting block, below the paste and the waterline, working by touch alone. It finds the gap at the far edge, hesitates once, and sets the board edge-first. The wood takes the weight with a creak that runs up through the stone, and the thin end beds into the heap of pale rubble.

You draw a breath into your lungs and let it out through your nose, quiet.

The far edge of the block is open a palm's breadth now, and the board holds it. It won't hold a man's weight or a careless step, but it will hold the stone while Bram eases off the iron. The spectral hand fades out above the water, and the chalk dust drifts from your fingertips like smoke from a spent wick.

Below, the paste has slackened again, brownish now where the water is turning. A thin, grey-brown sludge rises out of the gap and spreads over the surface by the block's end, very slowly. Pel's breathing in the water is loud and steady, and his leg has come back enough that he can turn his body toward the inner wall.

At the lip, Osric keeps counting, his voice low and even, a counterpoint to the seep and the creak of the ropes.

"Quite a trick with the hand." You hear it in his voice; it isn't mocking. "I saw a woman who could light candles without a taper once. She was hung in the Gate for a witch."

He says it to your back, not to the hole.

Where you are: at the inner lip of the hole, by the oak · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 12 — what does Sefa Marrin do?Sefa flexes the hand once, and the ghost of smoke curls from her fingers. "Lucky for you I can't light much more than that," she says to Osric, not turning. "You'll know a better trick: you held the rope and kept count."

She looks down into the hole again, where the far board holds the block and Bram's arms can rest. "Bram, ease off the iron when you're safe to. Pell, out clean and fast now, one pull steady." Her voice is low and level, no command to the water or the stone, only to the men.

Then she crosses the few feet to the oak and lays both hands on Pell's taut line, feeling the strain run from the trunk into the bark, and sets her feet, ready not to heave but to take the shock if Pell comes clear.
presses.reply:
Thanks. Working blind by the feel of the hand fits Sefa, and so does the steadiness of what she says to the men below. Here is how I'll take it when the card goes on.

**These stand as written, because they are Sefa's:**
- How she works the hand: Osric's board slid along the block's face below the waterline, the gap found by touch, the board set edge-first.
- Her breath, and letting the hand go once the work is done.
- Her words to Bram ("ease off the iron when you're safe to") and to Pell ("out clean and fast now, one pull steady").
- Crossing to the oak, both hands on Pell's line, feet set to take a shock rather than heave.

- **Whether the board seats and holds.** That is exactly what the waiting card decides. After [Onward] the narration tells it as an event either way.

scenes.narration:
Bram's call goes up the shaft in short bursts, all he can spare while his back is on the iron. The bar is bowed under him and the lump of chalk grinds under the shaft every time he breathes. Under the milky water the slab that pinned Pell's instep has slid down the heap, and it lies against Bram's boot now, loose. On the near side of the block the water churns as Pell draws his leg back. Bram can't see how far it went.

At the inner lip Osric's voice hasn't changed. "Forty. Forty-five." Bram's *still awake* reaches him, and so does *him first, then me*. He keeps counting and adds two words between the numbers. "Fifty. Heard you."

Sefa takes a half-step along the inner edge, keeping well off the bad lip, and the pale hand forms again over the hole like dusted glass. It drops to the top of the block, closes on Osric's split board where it lies across the cut sun, and lifts it clear. She brings it low along the face of the stone, past the turning case, past Bram's shoulder and his white knuckles on the iron, to the far long edge where the block stands up off the heap.

The gap is about an inch, a little more under the bar. The board is a split length of old timber, thicker at one edge than the other, and the paste is already creeping back into the gap from both sides.

Sefa doesn't force it. She turns the board in the hand's grip until the thin edge leads, then lays it flat against the block's underside and feeds it in. The first push meets paste and stops. She draws it back a finger's width, finds the firmer rubble a little lower down, and slides it in along that. The split timber goes under the raised far edge beside the bar's tip, a hand's length deep, and beds itself with its flat face up against the white stone. A grey bloom of paste squeezes out round it and clouds the water. Sefa feels the wood go stiff in the hand's grip as the weight starts to find it. She lets go, and the hand fades over the water.

"Sixty," Osric says.

Bram feels the change through the iron, the same as last time. He lets the bar up a finger's width. The far edge comes down after it a hair and stops on the board with a soft wooden creak. It doesn't move after that. He eases off a little more, then all the way. The block stays up on both sides: the near corner on Sefa's cake of crust, the far edge on Osric's board, the middle standing clear of the heap where the slab used to lie. Bram's arms hang at his sides in the cold water. His shoulders have stopped burning, and now they throb.

The counting stops. Osric doesn't say anything to mark it.

Down in the drift Bram blinks, and the warm heaviness behind his eyes comes and goes with it, a little slower to go than before. On this side of the block, away from the light, the sweet bakehouse smell sits thick on the water. The loose slab lies against his boot. Past the block's far end the old pit-prop lies half-sunk along the wall, and the drift runs on into the dark toward the seam. The seep keeps up its trickle somewhere along it.

Up at the inner lip Osric still has the lifeline in both fists. He looks at Bram's face, then at the water round Bram's chest, then at the sun, which is close to its height now over the white faces of the cut. Sefa stands on the inner edge with the oak a step behind her. Both ropes are in her sight, and the hot light is full on her neck.

Under the milky water the slab that pinned Pell's instep has slid down the heap, and it lies against Bram's boot now, loose. On the near side of the block the water churns as Pell draws his leg back. Bram can't see how far it went.

At the inner lip Osric's voice hasn't changed. "Forty. Forty-five." Bram's *still awake* reaches him, and so does *him first, then me*. He keeps counting and adds two words between the numbers. "Fifty. Heard you."

Sefa takes a half-step along the inner edge, keeping well off the bad lip, and the pale hand forms again over the hole like dusted glass. It drops to the top of the block, closes on Osric's split board where it lies across the cut sun, and lifts it clear. She brings it low along the face of the stone, past the turning case, past Bram's shoulder and his white knuckles on the iron, to the far long edge where the block stands up off the heap.

The gap is about an inch, a little more under the bar. The board is a split length of old timber, thicker at one edge than the other, and the paste is already creeping back into the gap from both sides.

Sefa doesn't force it. She turns the board in the hand's grip until the thin edge leads, then lays it flat against the block's underside and feeds it in. The first push meets paste and stops. She draws it back a finger's width, finds the firmer rubble a little lower down, and slides it in along that. The split timber goes under the raised far edge beside the bar's tip, a hand's length deep, and beds itself with its flat face up against the white stone. A grey bloom of paste squeezes out round it and clouds the water. Sefa feels the wood go stiff in the hand's grip as the weight starts to find it. She lets go, and the hand fades over the water.

"Sixty," Osric says.

Bram feels the change through the iron, the same as last time. He lets the bar up a finger's width. The far edge comes down after it a hair and stops on the board with a soft wooden creak. Bram's arms hang at his sides in the cold water. His shoulders have stopped burning, and now they throb.

Down in the drift Bram blinks, and the warm heaviness behind his eyes comes and goes with it, a little slower to go than before. On this side of the block, away from the light, the sweet bakehouse smell sits thick on the water. The loose slab lies against his boot. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops with the point of the sword against the packed gutter and thinks like a lockpick, not a miner: you don't dig a stuck pin out. You go round it.

"Bram — nothing of me is under that stone now. Let it down *on your count*, slow, onto the mud, and get your weight off the iron before your arms go. Then out of the water. I mean it — you've been breathing this as long as I have." He waits for the stone to be down before he moves again.

Then he sheathes the shortsword, reaches back into the pack still on his shoulders and comes out with a dagger. "Heel's set in a gutter like it's been mortared. I'm not digging that out blind. I'm cutting the boot." He feeds the dagger down along his shin, finds the top of the boot by touch, and starts opening it — down the inside seam from the cuff to the ankle, slow, point turned away from the skin, the way you'd slit a purse string without the owner feeling it. Laces, then leather. When the upper's open to the heel counter, he works his toes free, draws the foot up and out of the boot like a hand from a glove, and leaves the boot in the gutter for the quarry to keep.

"Hale, keep counting. Something else now — count me the seasons. How many cases of salt since you took the keys." The question's for himself as much as the man; a number to hold on to while his eyes want to close.

The moment the foot's clear he hauls on the oak rope, gets his good knee on the board, and goes for the far wall — back, foot and both arms, a yard at a time, head up out of the sweetness.

You wait until the stone is down before you move. Then you ask Hale to count you the seasons, meaning how many cases of salt he has shipped since he took the keys.

The count comes down the hole while you speak: fifty-five, then sixty. Wood creaks softly on the far side of the block as it takes weight, and the count stops. Under your palm the cut sun is dead still. No iron grinds anywhere. The stone sits on its chocks and rests on no part of you.

You sheathe the shortsword. Your pack is still on your shoulders, sodden through. You get one hand into it by feel and bring out the second dagger. The cold has got into your fingers and they are slow on the grip. The sweetness rising off the stirred water is thick now, and the heaviness you have been holding off with your knee comes up behind your eyes again.

presses.text:
The dagger's in his fist and the boot cuff's under his fingertips, and then the count has stopped and he can't remember what number Hale got to. That's the thing that tells him. Not the eyes — the number.

"Bram." It comes out thicker than he means it to. "Going under. It's the water, not the cold." He gets the dagger's point down the inside of the boot cuff and makes the first cut — laces, a hand's length of leather — before his wrist forgets what it was doing. Then he does the one thing left that's worth doing: he takes a second turn of the oak rope round his forearm and locks his fist over it, so his own arm will hold his head up when the rest of him won't.

"Rope's round my arm. Don't let anyone cut — the boot. Cut the boot, not the —"

His chin finds his chest. The dagger is still in his hand, under the water, because he's a Lower City boy and you don't drop a blade. The last thing he's aware of is cold, sweet breath on his knuckles from the gap behind the plaster, and Hale's flat voice somewhere above saying a number he doesn't catch.

presses.text:
The second cut never comes. His fingers find the slit he made and can't tell leather from lace from his own numb shin; the dagger's edge wanders, catches, and he stops it because he doesn't know what it's touching. His hand knows the rule even when his head doesn't — point away from skin, and if you can't feel skin, you don't cut.

"Can't—" The word's barely a word. "Can't feel it. Boot's still on. Bram, somebody's hands —"

His fist tightens on the two turns of oak rope round his forearm. The dagger stays in the other hand, down in the white water, held by habit alone. His head drops. The sweet cold breathes on his knuckles from the dark behind the plaster, and he lets it, because there's nothing left in him to argue.
presses.reply:
Thanks. Stopping the blade because he can't feel what it's touching is very much Pell, and it reads true. Here is how I'll take it when the card goes on.

**These stand as written, because they are Pell's:**

- His words: "Can't— Can't feel it. Boot's still on. Bram, somebody's hands —" Bram and Sefa hear them as spoken. How they answer is their players' call, in their own round.
- His fist tightening on the turns of oak rope round his forearm, and the dagger kept in his other hand under the water.
- His head dropping, and his choice not to fight the sweet cold breathing from behind the plaster.

**These are suggestions. The die and the world decide them:**
- **What the cut he did make has done.** The waiting card decides that. After [Onward], the narration tells what the blade's work came to as an event, whether the slit is enough to matter or not, within his choice to go no further.
- **What the drift's air does to a man who stops arguing with it.** A dropped head is Pell's choice. Whether he slips into sleep, how far, and how fast is the world's to say. The rope round his forearm counts for what it's worth.
- **What the others see and do.** Osric, at the lip, reacts as Osric would.

scenes.narration:
The count comes down the hole while Pell speaks. "Fifty-five. Sixty." Then a soft creak of wood takes weight on the far side of the block, and the count stops. Under his palm the cut sun is dead still. No iron is grinding anywhere. The stone is sitting on its chocks, and it isn't on any part of him.

He sheathes the shortsword. His pack is still on his shoulders and sodden through. He gets one hand into it by feel and comes out with the second dagger. The cold has got into his fingers and they're slow on the grip. The sweetness rising off the stirred water is thick now, and the heaviness he's been holding off with his knee comes up behind his eyes again.

The first part goes well. The laces part under the edge, and then the leather. He opens the upper a finger's length at a time, down the inside seam from the cuff to the knob of the ankle. Then the seam turns under toward the heel, where the leather is stiff and doubled and half-buried in the set paste, and he can't follow it any longer. His fingers don't tell him where the point is. They only tell him it's stopped. He leans on it a hair, the way you lean on a stuck pick. The blade jumps the thick stitching and goes into him instead, a hot sharp bite just under the ankle bone. He gets the point out at once. A thin thread of darker cloud winds up through the milky water. It's a shallow cut and it stings like fire, and his ankle is still where it was.

Then he tries the foot anyway. He gets his toes working inside the opened upper, and the front of the foot comes up a little in the slack leather. The heel doesn't. Feeling down inside the cut, he finds out why. The paste didn't stop at the outside of the boot. In an hour under the water it has worked in at the cuff and filled the heel of the boot around his own heel. That paste is softer than what's packed in the gutter, cold clay rather than mortar, but it's set enough to hold. With the stiff counter still standing whole around it, the heel sits in a cup of clay inside a cup of stone. The boot is open to the ankle now, but the foot still can't come out of it. The heel counter has to be cut away, or the clay inside it dug out with a narrow point, and his own skin is right there in the dark.

Up at the inner lip, Osric heard the question. Pell's lost the start of the answer in that grey moment, but the warden is still going. He isn't counting the cases themselves. He's going through the years, the way he'd read back a tally page, flat and low:

"…Six, none. Seven, one. Eight, none. Nine, none." Every year gets the same weight. "Ten, one. Eleven, none." It runs on like that, most years none and now and then a single case. At seventeen the count stops for a breath, longer than any of the others. Then he says "Seventeen, none" in the same voice and goes on. "Eighteen, one. Nineteen, two."

Then there's a short pause.

"This year. Spring, one. Summer, one. Thorn's makes three." His jaw works. "Twenty years. Eleven cases. Five of them since last winter."

He doesn't say what that means. He doesn't seem to know. He stays crouched at the timbers with the lifeline in both fists, and his eyes go to the dark water by Pell's ankle where the thread of blood is spreading.

The oak rope is wound round Pell's forearm and still holding him up. The block sits on its two chocks with the cut sun in a patch of light. The case turns slowly on its silk line overhead. Somewhere down the drift the seep trickles on, and the black gap behind the plaster keeps breathing its faint cold sweetness across his knuckles.

Your narration:
<<<
The count comes down the hole while Pell speaks. "Fifty-five. Sixty." Then a soft creak of wood takes weight on the far side of the block, and the count stops. Under his palm the cut sun is dead still. No iron is grinding anywhere. The stone is sitting on its chocks, and it isn't on any part of him.

He sheathes the shortsword. His pack is still on his shoulders and sodden through. He gets one hand into it by feel and comes out with the second dagger. The cold has got into his fingers and they're slow on the grip. The sweetness rising off the stirred water is thick now, and the heaviness he's been holding off with his knee comes up behind his eyes again.

The first part goes well. The laces part under the edge, and then the leather. He opens the upper a finger's length at a time, down the inside seam from the cuff to the knob of the ankle. Then the seam turns under toward the heel, where the leather is stiff and doubled and half-buried in the set paste, and he can't follow it any longer. His fingers don't tell him where the point is. They only tell him it's stopped. He leans on it a hair, the way you lean on a stuck pick. The blade jumps the thick stitching and goes into him instead, a hot sharp bite just under the ankle bone. He gets the point out at once. A thin thread of darker cloud winds up through the milky water. It's a shallow cut and it stings like fire, and his ankle is still where it was.

Then he tries the foot anyway. He gets his toes working inside the opened upper, and the front of the foot comes up a little in the slack leather. The heel doesn't. Feeling down inside the cut, he finds out why. The paste didn't stop at the outside of the boot. That paste is softer than what's packed in the gutter, cold clay rather than mortar, but it's set enough to hold. With the stiff counter still standing whole around it, the heel sits in a cup of clay inside a cup of stone. The boot is open to the ankle now, but the foot still can't come out of it. The heel counter has to be cut away, or the clay inside it dug out with a narrow point, and his own skin is right there in the dark.

scenes.narration:
Bram leaves the loose slab where it lies against his boot and starts back toward Pell. He keeps his shoulder to the sound wall the whole way, giving the board under the far edge and the crust cake under the near corner a wide berth. The water drags at his mail with every step. He holds the pinch-bar low in one fist, its tip down, well clear of both ropes. Round the far end of the block the light from the hole opens up again, and with it comes the cold, and with the cold comes the warm weight behind his eyes. It's slower to lift now when he blinks.

Halfway round, the heaviness tries to settle on him like a blanket over his shoulders. Bram doesn't let it. He bites down hard and fills his chest with the cold air coming down the shaft from the hole, not the sweet air off the water, and it clears. His head comes up sharp, the way it used to on the last watch before dawn when a wagon wheel creaked where no wagon should be. It doesn't feel like it's gone for good, only pushed back. For now he's thinking clearly.

His question goes down to Pell, and his calls go up the shaft to Sefa and to Hale.

He can see the answer to the first one before anyone gives it. The block's near side is open water now, and nothing of the stone lies over any part of Pell's leg. The leg runs out straight along the floor. At its end, the left boot is slit open down the inside from cuff to ankle, and its heel is sunk in the floor. A straight, square gutter is cut into the rock there, a hand wide, running along the drift, and the boot's heel is packed into it under grey paste that has set like mortar. A thin thread of darker cloud winds up from just under the ankle bone and spreads into the milk. The foot isn't clear, and no rope can bring it up yet.

Up at the inner lip, Osric has heard *help her haul him*. He doesn't touch Pell's rope where it runs to the oak.

"He's held," he says down the hole. "Heel's in the floor. I'll not haul a man that's held. Pull a leg out of its socket that way." He shifts his grip on Bram's lifeline. "Say when he's loose."

Then his eyes go to Bram's face, the same as they did to Pell's earlier, and stay there for a moment.

"Half an hour, you," he says. "Near enough."

He says nothing more. He stays crouched at the timbers with the hemp wound round his wrist and both fists closed on it. His shadow lies across the water beside the cut sun.

Bram stands at Pell's side of the block, with the water at his ribs and the bar in his fist, its tip down and clear of both lines. Under his boot the gutter runs on past Pell's heel, dead straight, the work of men who wanted water led somewhere. There's no current in it, and the water around him isn't going anywhere. Somewhere down the drift the seep keeps trickling. Overhead the canvas bundle turns on its silk line, and the sun's patch has slid on along the dark water past the block's far end.

 Bram's first try at shaking it off fails. The heaviness comes down over his eyes all at once, warm and thick as wool, and for the space of a breath his chin dips toward the milky water and his grip slackens on the bar. On the second try he throws it off: he jerks his head up, drags in a lungful of the cold air from the shaft, and his eyes clear. The bar is still in his fist and his feet are still under him, and he's awake.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps only as close as sound ground allows, keeping low near the oak, and checks that Pell's line lies clear of the crumbling lip and the turning case. Then she calls down, not loud, but clear through the chalky air: "Pell — if that leg's free, say so. We'll take your slack and you climb or we haul, whichever serves."

She shifts her grip on the rope, ready but not leaning into it. To Bram she says, "You've carried enough of that water. You're slower than you were. Out with the next man, not after him. The block's held on both sides."

Her eyes go once from Bram's face to the hanging case, then beyond it, into the dark mouth of the drift where the seep runs. "And keep a voice in that hole," she says, to whichever of them can still speak. "The quiet is what the old workings like."

scenes.narration:
Sefa keeps low by the oak and goes no closer than the grey drift timbers along the inner edge. She can feel the ground ring hard under her boots there. From this spot she can follow both lines.

Pell's rope runs off the oak in two turns and Osric's carter's knot. It crosses the inner timbers a forearm's width in from the edge and goes straight down the sound wall into the water. It lies well clear of the crumbling outer lip. Three feet to the right of it, on the bad side, Pell's silk rope runs over the broken prop, and the canvas bundle turns slowly on it below. The two lines don't touch anywhere. The oak rope is drawn hard and doesn't move. Nobody below is pulling on it, so there's no slack to take in. She keeps her hands on it anyway, loose, without leaning back.

From above, the drift is easier to read than from inside it. Pell lies along the near side of the block with his head and shoulders up on the rope. His leg runs out straight along the floor into milky water and disappears. A thin darker thread winds up through the milk near where his foot must be and spreads out. Bram stands beside him with the water at his ribs and the iron bar tip down in one fist. The sunburst block sits square on its two chocks with the cut rays turned up to the light. Past it the drift goes into the dark, and the seep trickles on somewhere down there.

Her words go down the hole, to Pell first and then to Bram. Whatever answer comes up the shaft belongs to the men below.

Osric is crouched on the timbers an arm's length from her, with Bram's lifeline wrapped round his wrist and held in both fists. He doesn't look round while she talks to them. When she says the old workings like the quiet, he turns his head and looks into the dark where the drift runs off toward the seam, and he takes his time about it.

"Not the quiet," he says. "The air."

He says nothing else. He looks up once at the sun, which is well up over the white faces of the cut now and still short of its height, then back down at Bram's face.

Sefa's shadow and his lie side by side over the water, beside the cut sun. The case turns a little on its silk line. On the white wall below the inner edge, the wet line sits a hair above the old dark stain, the same as it did a quarter of an hour ago.

 (Out of game: none of the three needed a roll. Each one is something Sefa says, and in the story she said all three. Pell's and Bram's answers come from their own players in their own scene, so I didn't play them here. The third line was spoken into the hole, and only Osric answered it: "Not the quiet. The air.")

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at the thread of his own blood winding up through the milk and puts the dagger away from the foot. Not sheathed — he doesn't trust his fingers to find the sheath — just up, hilt against his chest, point in the air. Rule's a rule: can't feel skin, don't cut.

"Done cutting myself." It comes slow and he makes each word land. "Boot's open to the ankle. Heel's in clay inside the counter — cup inside a cup. Needs the counter cut away from the *outside*, where someone can see what they're doing. Not me. Not blind."

He lifts his chin toward the far side of the block.

"Bram. If you're still in the water, come round. Take this." He holds the dagger out hilt-first across the stone, as far as the rope on his arm lets him. "I'll hold the foot dead still and keep talking. You cut the counter down the back seam, outside to in, and peel it. If you open me up a little doing it, do it anyway — a cut heel walks to Beregost, a drowned man doesn't. If you're out already, stay out and send the chalk hand. It can dig clay with no skin to mind."

Then, up to the lip, because the number is what's keeping him here: "Hale. Seventeen. You stopped." A breath. "What happened in seventeen?" He doesn't need the answer so much as he needs the man talking, and he's guessing that one will take a while.

He locks his fist on the two turns of oak, braces the bad knee on the board hard enough to hurt, and keeps his eyes on Hale's face up in the daylight — anywhere but the gap behind the plaster, which is still breathing on his hand.

scenes.narration:
Pell lifts the dagger off the foot and brings it up until the hilt rests against his chest and the point is in the air. He doesn't try for the sheath. The words come up the shaft slowly, one at a time, and each one gets there whole: *done cutting myself*, *cup inside a cup*, *from the outside, where someone can see*. Then he reaches across the wet white stone with the dagger held hilt-first, as far as the turns of rope on his forearm let him. It hangs over the cut sun in the light and stays there.

His last question goes up to the lip. He fixes his eyes on Osric's face in the daylight, grinds the bad knee into the board until it flares, and keeps his chin up out of the sweetness. All the while the cold sugar breath comes on his knuckles from behind the plaster, and the warm wool closes in behind his eyes again.

Pell holds on. The wool comes right up to the backs of his eyes. He doesn't let it in. The knee does it, and so does the light on Osric's grey beard: he fixes on that and won't look away. His head stays up and his fist stays shut on the oak rope. The heaviness sits there, near enough to touch, and gets no nearer.

Up at the timbers Osric has heard the question. For a while he doesn't answer it. He looks along the drift into the dark, where the seep runs, and Bram's lifeline creaks once in his fists.

"Lost a cutter," he says. "Tobin Reed. Low cuts. Spring."

The keys at his belt clink as his arms draw in round the rope.

"Book says drink."

He doesn't say whether the book is right. He looks down at Pell's face, at the chin held up out of the milk, and keeps looking.

"Talk, then," he says. "You've stopped twice. I'll not have three."

The dagger hangs hilt-first over the cut sun. The thread of blood from under the ankle bone has spread and gone pale in the water. Behind the plaster the black gap breathes on, slow and even. The patch of sunlight has moved on along the dark water past the block's far end, and the wet line on the white wall hasn't moved.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Hold the haul. His boot heel’s wedged in a gutter.”

I steady myself beside Pell, keeping my face toward the fresh air from above.

“Pell, let’s leave the boot behind. Can you slip your foot out through that cut?”

I support his calf without pulling and feel around the trapped heel, checking whether the hardened paste holds only leather or reaches his ankle. If the slit boot will open enough, I gently peel it away from his foot.

If the paste prevents that, I use the pinch-bar’s tip to break it away from the **outside of the boot**, working from the gutter’s exposed end and keeping the iron away from his flesh. I don’t lever against his leg.

“Sefa, keep his head supported. Hale, we’re freeing the heel now. No pull until we say.”

scenes.narration:
Bram's word goes up the shaft first: *hold the haul*. At the inner lip the lifeline stays as it is in Osric's fists.

"Heard," Osric says. "No pull."

Bram works himself in beside the leg with the sound wall at his back and the light from the hole on his face. He breathes what comes down the shaft, not what rises off the water. He gets one hand under the calf and takes its weight without lifting, then runs the other down the shin into the milk. The slit Pell cut opens under his fingers from the cuff to the knob of the ankle, laces and leather parted cleanly. He tries to peel it. The upper folds back easily as far as the ankle, and then it stops. Below that the heel counter is whole: stiff doubled leather standing up round the heel like a cup. When he presses the outside of it, it doesn't give. Something packed inside it holds it rigid. Outside the counter is the gutter, square-cut stone a hand deep, and the grey paste filling it is hard as lime-mortar. Peeling won't do it. Both layers have to come away.

So he takes up the bar. He feels along the gutter with the tip until he finds a short stretch past the heel where the fall's packing thins out against open floor. That's the gutter's exposed end, where he can see a little and feel the rest. He sets the iron there, angled down the channel toward the boot and away from the ankle, and starts to chip.

The first strokes only skid. The paste is set so hard the iron rings on it the way it would on stone. Bram stops forcing it. He turns the bar a quarter so the tip bites into the seam between the packing and the gutter's square wall, where the stone is smooth and the paste never quite bonded, and leans in short and steady, the way he'd knock out a seized wheel pin. A chunk comes away. Then another. He works back along the channel toward the heel a finger's length at a time, chipping and pulling the loose crumbs out by hand, and keeps the iron angled down the gutter wall, never across it. The paste breaks along the stone in grey slabs. By the time his fingers find the boot again, the gutter beside the heel is open from the floor to the leather. The outside of the counter stands bare in the water, and the iron hasn't touched it once. Whatever still holds that heel, it isn't the stone now. It's the clay packed inside the counter, and the counter itself.

He's put everything into the work, and he hasn't said a word for a long time.

The heaviness doesn't come on slowly the way it did before. It's just there. His hands go still on the bar, and his chin drops toward the milk, and the warm wool closes over him. For a breath or two the drift is very far off.

Then the loop round his chest yanks tight under his arms and hauls him upright, and Osric's voice comes down the shaft hard and close.

"*Halloway.*"

Bram's eyes open on daylight. He's still on his feet, held up on the lifeline, and the water is lapping at his collarbone instead of his ribs. The bar has slipped out of his fist.
