messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa picks a dry splinter of wood from the sound timbers at her feet, small as a thumb. She cups it, murmurs a word, and the splinter begins to glow with a cool, steady light. She does not drop it. The spectral hand forms again, pale in the sun, takes the glowing splinter from her palm, and carries it down the wall clear of both ropes to rest on the flat of the block inside the carved sun.

"Light on the stone," she calls down. "Pell, if the foot will come free now, work it slow. If it's still held past the block, tell me where — I'll bring the light there."

She keeps one hand on Pell's rope and watches the water beneath the glow, searching for the thin dark thread of blood where his foot disappears.

scenes.narration:
Sefa picks a splinter of dry grey drift timber off the sound edge at her feet, no bigger than her thumb. She cups it and says the word, and the splinter lights up. It's a cool, steady white glow, plain in the sunshine and stronger in the shade below. The pale hand forms beside her, takes the splinter from her palm and carries it down past the grey timbers, well clear of the oak rope and the silk. It sets the splinter flat on the top of the block, in the middle of the carved sun.

The drift under the lip has been half in shadow all morning. Now there's light in it. The cut rays stand out sharp, each groove holding a thin line of shadow, and the ring of notches round them shows as clearly as letters on a page. The milky water near the stone lights up a little way down, enough for Sefa to see what she was looking for.

The leg runs out straight along the floor beside the block, and none of it is under the stone now. The boot is pale with paste and slit open down the inside from cuff to ankle, the leather folded back. Below the ankle the heel sits in a square gutter cut into the floor, and the gutter beside it has been chipped open. Grey slabs of broken packing lie along it, and the iron bar rests on the floor next to it. The stiff heel counter stands up whole round the heel like a cup. The thin dark thread winds up out of the milk from just below the ankle bone, where the leather was opened. It's the boot that holds him now, not the stone. That spot is a forearm's length beyond the edge of the block, in open water, and the light reaches it.

Bram is standing by the sound wall in the light, upright on the lifeline. The water is at his collarbone. Not long ago his chin went down toward the milk, and Osric hauled the hemp tight and barked his name. That was a minute ago, and the line has stayed hard and straight since then.

Then something else lights up.

It doesn't come from the splinter. It comes from behind the plaster, in the black gap no wider than a knife blade at the back of the empty socket. A glow shows there, and its colour is different. It isn't the splinter's cool white. It's milky, like lamplight through chalk-glass or a candle behind a shell. It wasn't there before her light touched the stone. It brightens slowly, the way a wick takes, and then it holds, faint and even, pulsing very slightly in time with nothing Sefa can name.

At her belt, the Book of Shadows is warm through the leather. Its pages are always faintly warm. They aren't usually this warm.

Osric has seen it too. He's crouched at the timbers with Bram's lifeline wound round his wrist, and he turns his head from Bram's face to the socket and stays turned toward it longer than he has looked at anything this morning. His keys clink once as his arms draw in round the rope.

"That's behind the wall," he says. "Nothing's behind the wall."

He looks at Sefa's empty palm, then at the glowing splinter in the cut sun, then back at the gap.

"Yours, is it?"

He doesn't wait for an answer before he looks back at Bram's face, and the hemp stays tight in his fists.

The pale hand hangs open over the water, waiting on her. The splinter's white light lies across the sunburst. Behind the plaster, the milky glow keeps up its slow, even breathing. Up on the track the sun is high and hot on the back of Sefa's neck, and it isn't noon yet.

 Sefa keeps her left hand on Pell's rope where it runs off the oak. The hemp under her palm stays hard and still, and the light shows her the thread of blood rising from the slit leather just under his ankle bone, a forearm's length past the edge of the block.

(Out of game: none of the three needed a roll. Light and Mage Hand are cantrips that simply work, spotting the foot in a lit pool from right above was there to see, and holding the rope is just holding it.)

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell talks. It's what the man asked for, and it's the only tool left he can work with both hands numb.

"Talking. Tobin Reed, spring of seventeen, low cuts, book says drink." His voice comes thick but he keeps it going, like a man feeding rope out hand over hand. "I'll tell you what the book says about me, Master Hale. Lower City, roofs over the Wide. Guild runner at fifteen — that's a boy who carries what he's told and doesn't ask what's in it. Out at twenty. Paid my debt in coin, and the thing they teach you doing that is a man who won't go down a certain hole and won't say why isn't a coward. He's a man who's been down it once." He wipes his face with the back of the rope-wound forearm. "Reed didn't drown drunk. He went heavy-headed in the sweet water and the book got a tidy word. Same as the lads got short shifts and no reason, and you got a seal and no wages."

He's listening to himself for the moment the words stop coming — that's the sign — and while he listens, he moves. The clay's inside the boot, Hale said the gutter's open now; whoever dug it, the cup of stone is gone and only the cup of leather is left. A boot can come out of a gutter whole.

He stops trying to get the foot out of the boot. He takes the boot and foot as one thing. Good foot braced on the block's flank, fist locked on the oak, he draws the whole leg straight up through the water — knee bent, slow, the slit upper flapping — hauling boot and heel and clay together up out of the groove like a cork. If the heel counter catches the gutter's lip, he rolls the ankle a hair and tries again; if it needs more lift than one leg gives, he lets the rope take him and pulls with his whole weight hanging off the oak.

"Count me, Hale. Fives. If I miss one, say it louder." Then, between numbers, still working: "Thorn's not getting dye-salt. Eleven cases in twenty years, five since winter, and a Gate steward who's stopped paying the only man who'd notice. I'll tell her that in my words. But I'll need to be standing up when I do it."

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10

Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest

Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Pell slows before the yard and lets you lead, keeping his hands loose and empty away from his sword. Low, he tells you and Sefa that the place is empty and the man isn't surprised to see you. He says you should do the talking, Sefa should stay near him, and he'll watch the high ground. Sefa remarks quietly that someone waited for your arrival and that things should stay civil, not friendly. After you speak to the warden, she stops farther back, raises an empty hand, and calls out that you are sent by the apothecary Maela Thorn of Beregost, asking if he is the warden of Whitestone.

The yard is bigger up close than it looked from the bend. White dust lies over everything, fine as flour. The terraces above are bare, with only swallows working the cracks. The sheds stand shut, and the two lower ones are barred from outside. The tools by the lower cut weren't dropped: the hammers lie with their heads together and the wedges are stacked beside them. There's no blood and no drag marks. The traces on the cart were unbuckled, not cut, and the straps hang neatly over the shaft. A broad churned band of bootprints runs from the yard down the cart track, a dozen men or more walking together, not running, a day old by the dust in the heel-marks, with the hoofprints of a single mule beside them.

The house has its front shutters open, and one side window is closed. By the door there is one stool, one tin cup on the sill and one pair of boots, the ones on the man wearing them.

You stop a few paces short of the doorway and leave the man room. He looks at your shield, then your sheathed sword, then Pell's loose hands, and last at Sefa. He takes his time.

"Hale," he says. "Osric Hale. I'm the warden."

He looks past you at the cart for a moment, as if it had asked the question.

"Nobody's hurt. They walked. Noon bell yesterday, the lot of them." He shifts his weight in the doorway but doesn't step out of it. "Thorn's case is inside. Sealed, like she wanted."

His keys clink once as his arms tighten across his apron.

"She pay for it? Because somebody's been paid for that salt. Three weeks I've had no wages from the Gate for my men, and no answer to my letters. The case stays where it is till I know whose pocket that money's sitting in."

Behind him, thin grey smoke keeps rising from the chimney into a sky already white with heat.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: Whitestone quarry yard, a few paces from the warden's doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa says to you, low, that Hale is no bandit but a man holding the last thing he has to bargain with. Then, hands open and voice steady, she tells Hale that nobody paid you to take the case against his will and that you carry no wages from the Gate. You will be in Beregost by sunset, she says, and can put his question to Maela Thorn about whose pocket the money is in. That is more than three weeks of letters have achieved. She adds that a sealed case kept there past nightfall feeds nobody, and asks him to let it go with you and let his question go with it.

Pell, watching the yard, looks once toward the pair of lower sheds, both barred on the outside, and then toward the chimney. He murmurs to you and Sefa that Hale is holding the case against the Gate, not against you, and that nobody bars sheds from the outside for the sake of storing tools. Then he steps up just behind your shoulder and tells Hale in an even voice that you are hired carry, not Thorn's counting-house, that nobody has sent his wages, and that Thorn's buyer leaves Beregost at sunset. He offers to carry a sealed letter from Hale with the case and put it in Thorn's hand. Otherwise, he says, you all sit while the sun goes and nobody is paid. He asks what is in the two barred sheds.

Osric Hale listens to all three of you without interrupting. He gives your shield the same look as before, and takes longer over Sefa's face.

"Who owes them," he says. "House Vandarren. Gate patriars. Whitestone's theirs on paper." He reaches back without turning and takes a folded paper off a shelf just inside the door. He doesn't step out of the doorway. He holds it out at arm's length for you to read but doesn't let go.

It's a carter's order, in a clerk's neat hand on good paper: by the steward of House Vandarren, one case, sealed, of the rose salt from the low workings, to be held at Whitestone for M. Thorn of Beregost or her carriers. Account settled with the House's agent, A. Penn, at the Gate.

"Settled," Osric says. "Says so there. Three weeks back. Same week my wages stopped." He folds the paper into his apron. "So she paid. Penn took it. My lads got nothing."

He looks at Pell, then down at the barred sheds, as if they had asked.

"Saws and the house's good irons in the near one. I barred it. The lads were angry, and angry men take things they'll hang for." His keys clink as his arms fold tighter. "Other's the old cutting-shed. Shut. Nobody works in it now."

He says nothing more about it.

Sefa's offer is the one he is still turning over. He watches her the way he watched the cart, and she holds his eye. She has promised no wages and pretends to be nothing she is not, and in the end that is what he can't argue with. Something in his shoulders gives a little, though his arms stay folded.

As you lean into the iron, the bar bites. For a breath the lump of chalk under the shaft grinds and you think it will crumble. It holds. You put your whole back into it, the way you once got a loaded wagon off a broken wheel on the Way, and the block answers. It is slow, the way a ton of stone always is. The far long edge comes up off the heap with a deep sucking sound, and the whole block tilts on Sefa's chock under the near corner, rising through the middle where it had sat lowest. You get an inch, then a little more, and you feel the iron telling you that's all there is. Under your hands something gives way: the crust slab, its weight suddenly gone, grates in the rubble and settles. The block isn't bearing down on it now. The stone stands up off the slab through the middle, as high as the bar can raise it, and it stays there while you keep your weight on the iron.

Then the count starts again, and it starts shorter than the first time. Your shoulders had only just stopped burning from the first hold. Sefa's warmth has gone out of your arms. In the milky water round the slab the paste is already slumping, a slow grey creep into the new gap under the stone from both sides. Osric's board lies flat on top of the block over the cut sun, a hand's reach from either side, and nobody has it in hand yet. Both your hands are on the bar.

At the inner lip Osric has stood up out of his crouch. He doesn't come past the timbers. He has the lifeline in both fists now instead of one, and his eyes are on your face, not on the stone.

Sefa stands by the oak with her hand on the bark and both ropes in sight. The sun's patch has slid off the plaster and onto the dark water beyond the block's far end. On the white wall the wet line hasn't moved.

Round 11 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa answers from above that you should keep holding, five more heartbeats at the iron, and that she'll get the board in beneath the far edge. She keeps one hand on the oak and sends her spectral hand out over the hole. It lifts Osric's board and carries it down along the face of the block. She calls that it's coming in on your far side, and tells Pell to work his leg free slowly, and not before she says so.

Your call goes up the shaft in short bursts, all you can spare with your back on the iron. The bar is bowed under you and the lump of chalk grinds under the shaft every time you breathe. Under the milky water the slab that pinned Pell's instep has slid down the heap and lies loose against your boot. On the near side of the block the water churns as Pell draws his leg back. You can't see how far it went.

At the inner lip Osric's voice hasn't changed. "Forty. Forty-five." Your answer reaches him, and between the numbers he says: "Fifty. Heard you."

The pale hand, like dusted glass, brings the board low along the face of the stone, past the turning case, past your shoulder and your white knuckles on the iron, to the far long edge where the block stands up off the heap. The gap is about an inch, a little more under the bar. The board is a split length of old timber, thicker at one edge than the other, and the paste is already creeping back into the gap from both sides.

Sefa doesn't force it. She turns the board until the thin edge leads and feeds it in. The first push meets paste and stops. She draws it back a finger's width, finds firmer rubble a little lower down, and slides it in along that. The timber goes under the raised far edge beside the bar's tip, a hand's length deep, and beds itself flat face up against the white stone. A grey bloom of paste squeezes out round it and clouds the water. The hand lets go and fades over the water.

"Sixty," Osric says.

You feel the change through the iron, the same as last time. You let the bar up a finger's width. The far edge comes down after it a hair and stops on the board with a soft wooden creak. It doesn't move after that. You ease off a little more, then all the way. The block stays up on both sides: the near corner on Sefa's cake of crust, the far edge on Osric's board, the middle standing clear of the heap where the slab used to lie. Your arms hang at your sides in the cold water. Your shoulders have stopped burning, and now they throb.

The counting stops. Osric says nothing to mark it.

You blink, and the warm heaviness behind your eyes comes and goes with it, a little slower to go than before. On this side of the block, away from the light, the sweet bakehouse smell sits thick on the water. The loose slab lies against your boot. Past the block's far end the old pit-prop lies half-sunk along the wall, and the drift runs on into the dark toward the seam. The seep keeps up its trickle somewhere along it.

Up at the inner lip Osric still has the lifeline in both fists. He looks at your face, then at the water round your chest, then at the sun, which is close to its height over the white faces of the cut. Sefa stands on the inner edge with the oak a step behind her.

You call down to Pell to ask whether his foot is clear, and up the shaft you tell Sefa to take up his rope and Hale to help her haul him onto solid ground, saying you will steady him from below. You add that your head is getting worse and that nobody should linger down here.

You can see the answer before anyone gives it. The block's near side is open water now, and no stone lies over any part of Pell's leg. The leg runs out straight along the floor. At its end the left boot is slit open down the inside from cuff to ankle, and its heel is sunk in the floor. A straight, square gutter is cut into the rock there, a hand wide, running along the drift, and the heel is packed into it under grey paste that has set like mortar. A thin thread of darker cloud winds up from just under the ankle bone and spreads into the milk. The foot is not clear, and no rope can bring it up yet.

Halfway round, the heaviness tried to settle on you like a blanket over your shoulders. You bit down hard and filled your chest with the cold air coming down the shaft, not the sweet air off the water, and it cleared. Your head came up sharp, the way it used to on the last watch before dawn when a wagon wheel creaked where no wagon should be. It feels pushed back, not gone for good.

Up at the inner lip, Osric has heard you. He does not touch Pell's rope where it runs to the oak.

"He's held," he says down the hole. "Heel's in the floor. I'll not haul a man that's held. Pull a leg out of its socket that way." He shifts his grip on your lifeline. "Say when he's loose."

Then his eyes go to your face, as they did to Pell's earlier, and stay there a moment.

"Half an hour, you," he says. "Near enough."

He says nothing more. He stays crouched at the timbers with the hemp wound round his wrist and both fists closed on it. His shadow lies across the water beside the cut sun.

You stand at Pell's side of the block, water at your ribs and the bar in your fist, tip down and clear of both lines. Under your boot the gutter runs on past Pell's heel, dead straight, the work of men who wanted water led somewhere. There is no current in it, and the water around you isn't going anywhere. Somewhere down the drift the seep keeps trickling. Overhead the canvas bundle turns on its silk line, and the sun's patch has slid on along the dark water past the block's far end.

Your first try at shaking off the heaviness fails. It comes down over your eyes all at once, warm and thick as wool, and for the space of a breath your chin dips toward the milky water and your grip slackens on the bar. On the second try you throw it off: you jerk your head up, drag in a lungful of the cold air from the shaft, and your eyes clear. The bar is still in your fist and your feet are still under you, and you are awake.

messages.text:
“Tools left out, cart left loaded,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa. “Something stopped work in a hurry.”

I walk into the yard toward the house, shield on my arm but sword sheathed, watching the sheds and lower cut as I go. I stop a few paces from the man, leaving his doorway clear.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I glance back at the idle cart. “Everyone all right here?”

I settle my shield at my side. “Three weeks unpaid is no small thing. But we’re hired carriers, Hale. Ninety gold between us on delivery, and nothing if we miss her buyer’s coach at sunset. I haven’t seen what she paid for the salt.”

I glance at the neatly stacked tools. “Your men left things in good order. I spoke too soon about trouble.”

Then I meet his eyes. “Who owes their wages, and who took payment for the case? If you’ve a bill or a letter tying the two together, let’s see it. What would satisfy you enough to let us carry it out today?”

“Thorn’s own hand,” I agree. “And we’ll ask her for an answer. That much we can promise.”

I step inside and read the tally-book’s receipt before signing, making sure it records collection of one sealed case for Maela Thorn, not an inspection of its contents. I check the cord, wax and corners for existing damage without disturbing the seal, then put my name and the day beside hers.

“If you’re nearly ready, walk back with us. Better company than your letters have had.” I nod toward the case. “Anything we need to know about carrying rose salt—keep it dry, keep it upright?”

“Dry, sealed, and keep to the track. Understood. Safe road, Hale.”

I wrap the case in my bedroll against dust and splashes, then lash it securely to my pack, leaving the sealed cord untouched. I settle the load before heading out.

“Burning Wizard if we have an answer for you,” I add at the door.

Outside, I say quietly to Pell and Sefa, “Let’s earn our pay. No shortcuts over old workings.”

I start back along the cart track, watching the footing and the road ahead.

I keep to the broad wheel-packed track around the bend, following the route the crew and mule took.

“Sing out when you want that load traded, Pell. Six hours is a long way to prove a point.”

I set a steady walking pace toward Beregost, keeping an eye on the scrub ahead and either side of the road. No detours unless something gives us cause to stop.

“Pell! We’ve got you. Is your leg pinned?”

I move toward the inner side of the track, away from the crumbling outer edge, and set my shield down. I pull out my hempen rope and tie a broad loop in one end.

“Sefa, call Hale! Tell him the track’s fallen in—we need help and a long timber.”

Staying back from the broken lip, I lower myself flat to spread my weight and try to feed the loop down within Pell’s reach.

“Under your arms if you can. Keep your head up. We’ll worry about the box later.”

I brace on intact ground and take up slack to help support him above the water, without trying to wrench him free of the stone.

“Sefa, secure my loose end round that oak while I keep his weight. Then fetch Hale—we need a lever, and the water’s rising.”

I keep steady tension on Pell’s rope, without hauling against his pinned leg.

“HALE! MAN DOWN! THE CART TRACK’S COLLAPSED!” I shout toward the house.

Then, down to Pell: “Rope’s staying with you. Can you see how the block’s caught your leg? Is there room beside you for someone to stand and lever it off?”

I look for a way down on the bank side, away from the broken prop and hanging case. I don’t put weight on the lip or start descending until the rope is anchored.

I ease Pell’s weight onto the anchored rope and get up on the bank side.

“I’ll take the bar down. Hale, help Sefa work the ropes from solid ground. If I go dull or stop answering, haul me out.”

I secure Hale’s rope to the oak, leaving enough length to tie a loop snugly around my torso as a lifeline. I leave my pack and weapons beside my shield.

“Sefa, lower the bar once I’m down. When Pell’s free, take up his rope—steady, not a jerk.”

I descend along the sound inner wall using the anchored rope, clear of the case and rotten prop, aiming for the old beam if it offers firm footing.

“Pell, tell me where it’s pressing. I’m coming beside you.”

Once down, I intend to use the pinch-bar with a firm fulcrum to lift the block just enough for Pell to withdraw his leg, keeping our hands out from underneath it.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“Stone’s up, Pell. Mud’s still holding you. Work your leg loose gently—I’ve got the weight.”

I keep both hands on the bar and hold steady.

“Hale! Need a flat wedge in this gap, two fingers thick. Sound wood or stone. Can you pass one to Pell? Don’t touch the fulcrum.”

“Sefa, take up Pell’s slack as he frees himself. Easy tension, not a hard haul.”

I keep talking so Hale can hear I’m alert. “Still steady. But we’ve less than a hundred count. Pell, can you reach the gap to chock it?”

“Getting heavy behind the eyes, Hale. Still thinking clear, but we need out soon.”

I take the sound board from the lip and keep the pinch-bar with me.

“Pell, where’s it still catching you? Point me to it.”

Keeping my lifeline clear, I move along the sound wall toward the far side, testing the floor before each step. I want to reach the remaining pressure point without disturbing Sefa’s chock or the prop holding the case.

If I can get firm footing there, I set the bar on a solid support to lift that side, with Hale’s board ready for Pell or Sefa’s hand to wedge into the gap.

“Sefa, be ready to chock this side. Then we draw him clear while both sides are held.”

“Up! Sefa—the board on top. Get it into this gap with your hand spell, now. Arms won’t last.”

I hold my weight on the bar, keeping the lift steady.

“Pell, stone’s off the slab. Work your foot clear while we’ve got it. Tell us the instant you’re free.”

I keep my eyes on the gap and call up to Hale, “Still awake. Once he’s loose, get him up first. Then me.”

“Pell, is your foot clear?”

I leave the loose slab alone and work back along the sound wall toward him, keeping clear of both chocks. If he’s free, I help guide him beneath the safe inner edge.

“Sefa, take up his rope. Hale, help her haul him onto solid ground. I’ll steady him from below.”

I keep the pinch-bar clear of the ropes and pass it up when I can, then follow Pell up the inner wall with my lifeline supporting me.

“Head’s getting worse. No more lingering down here.”

“Hold the haul. His boot heel’s wedged in a gutter.”

I steady myself beside Pell, keeping my face toward the fresh air from above.

“Pell, let’s leave the boot behind. Can you slip your foot out through that cut?”

I support his calf without pulling and feel around the trapped heel, checking whether the hardened paste holds only leather or reaches his ankle. If the slit boot will open enough, I gently peel it away from his foot.

If the paste prevents that, I use the pinch-bar’s tip to break it away from the **outside of the boot**, working from the gutter’s exposed end and keeping the iron away from his flesh. I don’t lever against his leg.

“Sefa, keep his head supported. Hale, we’re freeing the heel now. No pull until we say.”

private.text:
Sefa stepped up beside the oak, staying off the crumbling lip, and told you that you were the one who could get down there, but not in mail. She said to leave the shield and hauberk behind because the water was too close to risk their weight, to take Hale's bar, and to tie the rope under your arms and fasten it to the oak. She would watch the lip and feed you rope down to the old drift floor. She put a hand on your shoulder, and a thin, steady glow came up under her palm, warm as a lamp behind glass, and soaked into the rings of your mail. "Lantern, steady his hands," she said. Without turning, she told Osric Hale she wouldn't ask him down, only for his eye on the road and the rope, and asked him to stay until noon if he could. Osric didn't turn round either. "Said noon."

You lowered your end of Pell's rope until the oak took the full weight, then got up off your belly on the inner side. Your pack, longsword and javelins went down on the hard white ground beside the shield. You kept your chain mail on. You took Osric's coil from the foot of the oak, made it fast round the trunk below your own knot, and tied the other end in a snug loop round your chest under the arms.

"If I go dull or stop answering, haul me out," you said.

Osric looked at the loop, then at the hole, and took the slack of the lifeline in both fists. "Keep talking, then. I'll hear it stop."

You went over the inner edge with the rope in your gloves and your boots on the grey drift timbers. Below them the wall was sound, dry and square, just as it had looked from above. You walked yourself down it hand over hand, with the case turning on its silk rope off to your right, well clear. The cold hit you at the waist like a blow. Then your boots found the cut floor, and you stood with the water halfway up your ribs and the mail dragging at your shoulders. Down here the drift smells of wet chalk, and under that of something sweeter, close to the surface, like a flour bin left open. The old pit-prop lay along the wall about where it was said to be, a man's length of grey timber, half under the water.

Up top, Osric crouched at the inner lip with the lifeline wrapped once round his forearm. He reached the iron pinch-bar down at arm's length, holding the end. You took it out of the air above your head.

You waded to the near end of the block, where the white stone sits on the slumped heap of fall. You felt under the water for something hard to rest the bar on. The paste wouldn't do. Beside the heap you found a squared chunk of the road's crust, knocked the soft off it and bedded it on the cut floor, against the edge of the rubble. Then you set the bar's tip under the near corner of the block, laid the shaft across the chunk, and leaned your whole weight into it.

From above, Sefa calls down that the chock sits only under the near corner, so if you lift the middle you shouldn't trust it alone. She adds that a second sound board waits at the lip and that the pit-prop is on the floor along the far wall below you. Then she draws a slow breath and lets the Lantern's smallest blessing run off her wrist. It drifts down the shaft of daylight, past the turning canvas bundle, and settles on your forearms as a faint warmth under the cold, waiting for the next thing you put your strength to. She names it guidance, meant for whatever you lift next. Then, more quietly, she tells Osric to haul you out without waiting for her word if the road gives way any further. Osric doesn't look round. He says he wasn't going to.

You say your head is getting heavy behind the eyes, though you're still thinking clear, and that you need out soon. Osric answers at once. The lads did an hour at the low walls, he says, and then went up into the air, or they didn't come up right. You've had a quarter of that. He says nothing after.

You reach up past the grey drift timbers and take Osric's board off the lip. It is a forearm of split, dry wood, and it sounds true when you knock it. You keep the pinch-bar in your other fist. You ask Pell where it's catching him. The answer had already come up out of the water a moment earlier, when Pell called it to the top: the foot is under a slab of road crust on the far side of the block, past where Pell can reach.

So you go to the far side. You keep your back to the sound wall and the lifeline clear of the prop. You wade round the block's far end, where its white weight rests square on the level floor the old miners cut. The water drags at your mail with every step, and you test each one with your boot before you trust it. The floor here is firm stone, and the fall never reached it. Past the block's far end the old pit-prop lies along the wall, grey and half-sunk, and beyond it the drift runs back into the dark. The sweet smell is stronger on this side. It isn't by much, but you notice it. It's thicker away from the light and the hole, the way a bakehouse smells stronger the closer you get to the oven door.

You can't see the slab. The water is milk here too, stirred up from Pell's digging. You find the slab with your boot and then with one hand, reaching down along the block's long far edge. Along this stretch the block's underside doesn't sit on the floor. It sits on the heap of the fall, and in the heap is a flat edge of baked crust as wide as your palm, jammed under the stone. That's the slab. Its far edge is right here under your fingers, bedded in rubble and paste.

You can't push the bar's tip under the stone where the far end sits flat on cut floor. Where it sits on the rubble you can. You work your fingers in beside the slab and claw out a pocket of paste. You knock a seat into the heap with the bar's tip and find a fist-sized lump of hard chalk on the cut floor to bed the shaft across. You lay Osric's board flat on top of the block over the cut sun, where a hand from either side could take it. Then you set the tip, set your feet, and feel the warmth of Sefa's blessing gather in your forearms as you lean into the iron.

You leave the loose slab where it lies against your boot and start back toward Pell, keeping your shoulder to the sound wall the whole way. You give the board under the far edge and the crust cake under the near corner a wide berth. The water drags at your mail with every step. You hold the pinch-bar low in one fist, tip down, well clear of both ropes. Round the far end of the block the light from the hole opens up again, and with it comes the cold, and with the cold comes the warm weight behind your eyes. It is slower to lift now when you blink.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Round 1 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell slows before the yard and lets Bram go in front, keeping his hands loose and empty away from his sword. Low, he tells you and Bram that the place is empty and the man isn't surprised to see you. He says Bram should do the talking, that you should stay near him, and that he'll watch the high ground. Bram murmurs that tools were left out and the cart left loaded, then walks toward the house with his shield on his arm and sword sheathed. He stops a few paces from the man, leaves the doorway clear, gives his name, says Maela Thorn sent the three of you for a sealed case of dye-salts, and asks if the man is the warden. The moment stretches, and then Osric Hale's arms come down from his chest. He draws a long breath through his nose, the way a man does when he has finished turning something over.

"Leave together or not at all," he echoes, but now he means the three of you, the case and his letter.

He steps back from the doorway only as far as he needs to, and gestures — not quite a wave — for you to come inside. "Then I'll write it. You'll wait while I do."

The house is small and spare: a worn table, one chair, a hearth burning low, a shelf of accounts and cupboards painted the same grey as the quarry dust on everything. The case already stands on the table, a squat wooden chest banded in iron, its seal a disc of hard blue wax stamped with a hooked thorn. Beside it, Hale sits, dips a nib, and writes with the slow care of a man who does not write often.

"I'll put your name," he says without looking up. "The dark-haired woman. And the case goes to no one else in Beregost but Thorn's own hand. If they turn you back at the shop, you keep it and send for me."

He writes a page, folds it twice, and seals it with plain brown wax and his thumb. He does not hand you the case yet.

"The letter's for Olek, in Little Calimshan — by the spice stair, ask for him." Osric holds the letter out to you. "He knows the whole account of it. If the Gate's still deaf by the full moon, Olek has what he needs to make the Vandarrens listen from a different side."

Only then does he stand, lift the case from the table by its handles, and set it into Bram's arms rather than yours, with a nod that might be to both of you.

"Watch the road down by Bram's Crossing," he says. "Some of my lads were talking of the old cutting-shed before they went. There are men in this country who'd take that case from a carrier for half what Thorn paid."

He steps out into the yard behind you, and the white light closes around you all again.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet

Round 9 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

You stop working at the foot and lift your chin to the light. You breathe through your nose, and the yawn slowly drains out of your jaw.

While you're calling up to Bram, the drift changes around you. The creak of the iron stops. A moment ago something pale and see-through went past over the water, a hand the colour of chalk dust carrying a flat cake of crust, and now it's gone. Under the near corner of the block there's a small gritty crunch. Then nothing. You set your palm flat on the cut sun and the stone is cold and dead still. It isn't trembling the way a held lift does. It's sitting on something.

You work the fallen board tighter behind your back and take a turn of the rope round your forearm. The hemp is wet and rough. If your head nods now, your own arm holds you up. Your foot is still pinned flat across the instep under the middle of the block, exactly as before.

Under your hand, the black gap behind the plaster is a finger's length from your knuckles. There's air in it, barely there, a breath on wet skin and colder than the drift. It carries the same sweetness, flour and sugar, a little stronger than off the water.

At the inner lip Hale hasn't moved. Your orders and your warning about the grit and the yawning pass him by. His eyes stay on your face.

"Yours is on the oak," he says. "I've his." He moves his wrist an inch so you can see the hemp wound round it, and it isn't your rope. "Oak won't let go."

Then your question reaches him. He looks along the drift into the dark before he answers, the way he looked at the cart this morning.

"Stone. White stone, cut and squared. Beregost had it, and the Gate when the Gate paid. Lime, when the kilns still ran." A pause. "Salt. A case a season, off the low walls, when an order came. Men picked it by hand. Short shifts."

That's all he gives. Then, because you yawned, he adds more than you asked.

"Short, because they got slow. I said. Heavy-headed." His jaw works. "Don't sleep down there."

He says nothing else. He stays crouched with the lifeline round his wrist. His shadow lies over the water by the sunburst, and the pink dust turns slowly through it.

The seep trickles in the dark. The patch of sun has moved off the cut rays onto the plaster below the socket. The waterline on the white wall sits where it was, and the wall above it is still wet.

The first part goes well. The laces part under the edge, and then the leather. You open the upper a finger's length at a time, down the inside seam from the cuff to the knob of the ankle. Then the seam turns under toward the heel, where the leather is stiff and doubled and half-buried in the set paste, and you can't follow it any longer. Your fingers don't tell you where the point is. They only tell you it has stopped. You lean on it a hair, the way you lean on a stuck pick. The blade jumps the thick stitching and goes into you instead, a hot sharp bite just under the ankle bone. You get the point out at once. A thin thread of darker cloud winds up through the milky water. It's a shallow cut and it stings like fire, and your ankle is still where it was.

You try the foot anyway. You get your toes working inside the opened upper, and the front of the foot comes up a little in the slack leather. The heel doesn't. Feeling down inside the cut, you find out why. The paste didn't stop at the outside of the boot. In an hour under the water it has worked in at the cuff and filled the heel of the boot around your own heel. It is softer than what's packed in the gutter, cold clay rather than mortar, but it's set enough to hold. With the stiff counter still standing whole around it, your heel sits in a cup of clay inside a cup of stone. The boot is open to the ankle now, but the foot still can't come out. The heel counter has to be cut away, or the clay inside it dug out with a narrow point, and your own skin is right there in the dark.

Up at the inner lip, Osric heard your question. You lost the start of his answer in that grey moment, but he is still going. He isn't counting the cases themselves. He goes through the years the way he'd read back a tally page, flat and low: "…Six, none. Seven, one. Eight, none. Nine, none." Every year gets the same weight. "Ten, one. Eleven, none." It runs on like that, most years none and now and then a single case. At seventeen the count stops for a breath, longer than any of the others. Then he says "Seventeen, none" in the same voice and goes on. "Eighteen, one. Nineteen, two."

Then there is a short pause.

"This year. Spring, one. Summer, one. Thorn's makes three." His jaw works. "Twenty years. Eleven cases. Five of them since last winter."

He doesn't say what that means. He doesn't seem to know. He stays crouched at the timbers with the lifeline in both fists, and his eyes go to the dark water by your ankle where the thread of blood is spreading.

The oak rope is wound round your forearm and still holding you up. The block sits on its two chocks with the cut sun in a patch of light. The case turns slowly on its silk line overhead. messages.text:
Pell slows a half-step before the yard proper and lets Bram take the lead on the track — the man in chain mail is the one a warden expects to talk to. He keeps his hands loose and off his sword, visibly empty.

While they walk in, he isn't looking at the warden. He's reading the yard: the sheds and their doors, the terraces above for anyone lying flat, the spoil heaps, the ground around the dropped tools — footprints, blood, dragged marks, anything that says *why* a quarry crew puts its hammers down and walks off mid-morning. And the house itself: shutters open or closed, how many sets of boots by the door.

Low, to the other two, not moving his lips much: "Place is empty and he's not surprised to see us. Bram, you talk. Sefa, stay near me. I'll watch the high ground."

Then he waits for the warden to speak first.

Pell doesn't move his eyes from the yard while Hale talks. When the man finishes, he glances once at the two lower sheds — barred from outside — and then at the chimney, and only then at Hale.

Low, to Bram and Sefa, barely moving his mouth: "He's not holding the case against us. He's holding it against the Gate. We're just the nearest hands. And someone barred those two sheds from the outside before the crew left — you don't do that to keep tools in."

Then, a step behind Bram's shoulder, still not crowding the doorway, in an even, Lower City voice:

"Master Hale. We're hired carry, not her counting-house — she pays us on delivery, same as she's likely to pay you, which is why she's in a hurry and you're not. Nobody's sent us with your wages, and nobody's going to send them to a quarry that's gone quiet." A small nod toward the cart track. "Thorn's buyer leaves Beregost for the Gate at sunset. If you've got letters that want answering, that coach is the fastest road your complaint has had in three weeks. Write it, seal it, we carry it with the case and put it in her hand with the salt. You've got our names and the apothecary's."

A beat. "Or we sit here while the sun goes, and tomorrow nobody's paid at all — not Thorn, not us, not you."

He tips his chin at the lower sheds, mild. "And what's in the two you barred?"

Pell stays in the doorway a moment longer than he needs to, then steps in sideways — he doesn't like to stand in doorways with his back to a yard. He doesn't go to the table. He goes to the case, crouches, and looks before he touches: the cord, how the knot's tied, whether the wax sits on the knot or beside it, whether the seal's edge has the little lifted lip you get when someone warms it and sets it back. Then he lifts the case an inch by one iron corner to feel the weight and whether anything shifts inside. He's quiet about it, the way he'd check a lock before trusting it.

"Seal's a Vandarren house seal?" he asks Hale, without looking up. "Same as on your order?"

To Bram, low: "You sign. Your name's the one that's been on a caravan manifest before, and I'd sooner mine stayed out of a Gate house's book." A glance at the open tally-book, not to read it, just to see how many pages back the last entry is.

Then, still quiet, to Sefa and Bram: "We've got maybe nine hours of light and six of road. Case, letter, and go. Whatever's in the cutting-shed is his business and the lads'. We're paid for a box."

He stands, and to Hale, plain: "You walk at noon, you'll be an hour behind us. If you want it, we'll find you at whatever tavern the lads are drinking in before we hand Thorn her answer, so you hear it first." He leaves it there — an offer, not a promise he'll chase.

Pell nods once to Hale — the only thanks the man's going to accept — and picks the case up by its iron corners, testing the heft again. Twenty-odd pounds; nothing for a mile, a shoulder-ache by the sixth.

"Bram, you've got the back for it, but a man with a shield and a box has no hands. I'll carry." He unslings his pack, pulls out the silk rope, and rigs a quick cradle round the case — two turns under, one over the lid clear of the wax, a loop long enough to go across his chest so it rides on his back and leaves both hands free. He wraps the bedroll's canvas round it first against damp and dust. Fast work; he's done it with heavier things off higher ledges.

"We go the track, not the lip. Hale says the ground's hollow and I believe a man who's walked it twenty years." A glance back at the two barred sheds as he settles the weight. Not his box, not his pay. He lets it go.

To Sefa, quiet: "Letter stays on you. Thorn's own hand, like he said — we don't put it down anywhere." To Bram: "You in front, me middle with the case, Sefa behind. If anything's on that track that wasn't this morning, I want to see it before it sees the box."

Then, at the door, to Hale: "Burning Wizard. We'll be there." And he steps out into the glare and starts down toward the cart track.

Pell gives the footpath one look as they pass its mouth — the sagging turf, the grass grown back, a dozen men and a mule who all knew better — and keeps his boots on the hard white of the cart track.

"That's the one," he says to the others, nodding at the dip without slowing. "Settles under you and you're in an old drift with twenty pound of salt on your back and no rope to climb. We take the bend."

He settles the case higher on his shoulders and falls into the long, even stride of a man who has a half-day of road and means to arrive. Every so often, without making a show of it, he checks behind: the thinning smoke, the quarry shelf, the track they've walked — anyone coming down after them, anyone who was waiting for the carriers to leave with the box. The dust on the cutting-shed's sill was unbroken; whatever Hale isn't saying about that shed, it's been shut a long while, and that's a Vandarren matter, not his.

To Sefa, after a while, quiet: "If Thorn's paid and Penn pocketed it, that's a Gate house's steward with his hand in the till, and we're the ones carrying the proof down a road. I'd like to be in Beregost before anyone thinks that through." He watches the scrub oak on either side as he says it.

He keeps the pace brisk and steady — no stops till the sun's well past noon, and then only for water.

Pell holds very still for a three-count, the way you do when you don't yet know what's broken. Breath. Fingers. Toes — the left ones move, under the stone. Good. Then he spits chalk and tips his head back to the hole.

"Don't come to the edge!" Not loud — the roof's timber and he doesn't trust it. "It's still going. Get back from it. Both of you." A beat to let them. "I'm in one piece. Hip and shoulder, nothing broken. Left leg's under a block, pinned, not crushed. Case is hanging off a prop a foot under the road — it's dry, don't touch it yet. Water's chest-deep and there's a seep running somewhere, so I'd like to not be here long."

He gets his hands under the water and feels along the block's edge where it meets his shin — how it's sitting, whether it's bedded on rock or on loose fall. Rock, he's not shifting two feet of dressed stone with Strength like his. Loose fall, he can dig the leg out from under rather than lift the block off. He starts scooping at whatever's under his calf, slow, working the leg a quarter-inch at a time, bracing his free foot against the block to push rather than pull. If it won't give, he'll try wedging a dagger-hilt and a chunk of fallen board under the near corner for a hair of lift.

Up at the hole, while he works: "Bram — the case is on *my* rope. Don't cut it loose to get me; I'd sooner it hang there till I'm up. Have you got rope? Or the cart's traces, back in the yard — they were unbuckled, not cut. Hale's got rope too, he'll be awake another hour. Sefa, you've got light that heals — if you can do that from up there, I'd take it. If you have to come down, come down the far wall from the fall, not through the hole."

Only then does he look properly at the block beside his face — the sun-disc, the notched ring, the old plaster. He wipes a wet thumb across the chisel marks.

"Hale said the ground was worked under since before his time." Quiet, mostly to himself. "He didn't say by who." He doesn't touch it again. One problem at a time.

[Onward]

Pell's hands come up out of the water with nothing but chalk-mud under the nails. The leg's bedded on rock, not fall — nobody's digging it out. He stops before he does the stupid thing and starts kicking.

"Not moving," he calls up, flat. "Block's sitting on stone, I'm just pushing water around. Sefa's right. New plan."

He takes Bram's loop as it comes down and gets it under his arms, snug across the chest, then gives it a tug to show it's seated. "That's me on your rope, Bram. Don't haul yet — if you pull me straight up with the leg under this, you'll keep the leg." He reaches for the biggest piece of fallen board within arm's length — a chunk of the road's old planking — and works one end of it down under the near corner of the block, where the stone sits proudest off the bottom. His dagger goes under the board's heel as a fulcrum.

"Here's how it goes. I lever the corner — a finger's width is all I need. The second it lifts, you take up the slack hard and I kick the leg out toward you, away from the block. If it drops back, it drops back on bottom, not on me. Count of three on my word, not before." A breath. "And Sefa — if that light's for me, now's good. I'll want the leg working when it's out."

He gets both hands on the board, braces his free boot against the block's flank, and waits for Bram's rope to go taut.

Pell lets the rope take his weight and stops fighting the stone. He's breathing hard; he makes himself slow it.

"Right. Listen, because I've got the numbers and you don't." His voice carries up flat and even, the way he'd report a lock that won't give. "Block's far end is on cut floor, near end's on the fall. It'll lift with a lever — there's a pit-prop six feet from me, man-long. But it wants one body on the lever with a rope taking its weight and one body in the water digging, and it's an inch at a time. Two of you, it's sunset. One of you, it's never." A beat. "And the water's coming up. Finger's width since I went in. I don't get till sunset."

He twists to look at the chimney, then back up at the hole.

"Hale's still in the house — bolt's across, he doesn't walk till noon. He's got timber, he's got rope, and he's walked over these drifts twenty years. He said some of them took water; he'll know where it comes from, whether there's a sluice or a lower drift it runs off to. Sefa — go. Run, don't walk. Bang the door till he opens it. Tell him the track fell in on the bend, his carrier's pinned in a drift under it, and the water's rising. Bring him and the longest beam he's got."

To Bram: "You hold. Don't come down, don't haul, just keep me high and keep the anchor honest. If the lip goes further, tell me before it goes."

Then, grimmer: "And when Hale's here, that's two hands on the lever and the dig. Which means one of you takes the box and walks. Six hours, light to spare. Thorn gets her salt, we get paid, and nobody's sunset was wasted on me." He doesn't say who. "Decide it between you while she's running."

He takes the chunk of board, wedges it behind his back against the drift wall so he can't slide if the rope slips, keeps his free boot braced on the block, and holds still. Only his eyes move — to the waterline on the white wall, and to the smooth plaster face behind the empty socket, which has no business being there.

Pell feels it before he hears anything — the vice on his shin eases by a hair, the block's weight going up off him into something creaking above the water. He doesn't wait to be told, and he doesn't ask how.

"It's up — *hold it there, Bram, don't breathe.*" He gets both hands under the water, down along his own calf, and claws the paste out from under it in fast double handfuls, not digging the block out any more, just making room for the leg. Then he pulls — knee bent, foot pointed, leg sliding back toward him along the floor the way you draw a blade out of a sheath, away from the near end where the block will drop. Slow, steady, no kicking. If it hangs up on the shin, he turns the foot and tries again; he's wriggled through tighter spaces than a gap under a stone.

The moment the foot clears, he hauls himself hand over hand up the dead rope a yard and gets his good knee on the fallen board, out of the block's reach. "Clear! Let it down, let it down easy."

Only then, hanging there, dripping, with the knee screaming, does he look up at Hale.

"Not for anybody." He says it back without heat. "Twenty years here and you've never seen the block that was mortared into the wall of your own drift, and you won't come down the low cuts, and the water smells like a baker's shop." He wipes his face. "I'm not asking. I'm climbing out of your hole and walking your box to Beregost. But when I carry your letter to Thorn, I'll have been in this drift, and she'll ask me what it was like. Tell me what to say about that." He tips his head at the plaster face with the knife-thin black gap behind it. "Or don't, and I'll tell her what I saw."

Then, up to Bram and Sefa: "Rope. I'm coming up the far wall, away from the broken lip. Case after me, on its own line — nobody leans out for it. And the knee's gone, so the long walk's going to be slower than I promised."

Pell stops trying to turn the foot. He's learned the shape of the trap now; grinding the ankle on the slab just spends what he's got.

The yawn frightens him more than the water does. He shakes it off, lifts his chin, and breathes through his nose up toward the daylight rather than the stirred milk around his chest.

"Hold the lift, Bram. Don't lower it, don't lift more — just hold. Calf's out. Foot's jammed under a slab of crust on the *far* side of the block, past where I can reach. Someone has to kneel in the water over there and dig it off my instep. That's hands, not strength." A beat. "Sefa. You're lighter than him and he's on the bar. Far wall, away from the broken lip, on your own line. Hale — you've got my rope. Don't let it off your wrist till I'm up. After that you go where you like."

Then, lower, so it carries to Sefa but not as a shout: "And listen before you come. The grit under my leg is the same pink as what's in Thorn's case, and the water's gone sweet with it — flour and sugar. I've been breathing it a quarter-hour and I just yawned fit to break my jaw. I don't think that's dye-salt. Keep your face out of the water, don't drink it, don't lick your fingers, and work fast. If I go quiet, slap me."

He gets the fallen board wedged tighter at his back, winds a turn of the lifeline round his own forearm so he can't slip under if his head nods, and sets his free hand on the block's upper face, right over the cut sun, to feel the moment it shifts.

To Hale, flat, not looking away from the plaster face and its knife-thin black gap: "Twenty years you've counted loads out of here. Loads of what, Master Hale?"

The chocked stone under his palm tells him before anyone says it: the bar's free. He puts that together with the pale hand he saw carrying crust.

"Sefa — that hand. The one that set the chock." He keeps his voice level, pitched up the shaft. "It's got no face to keep out of the water and no lungs to breathe this sweetness with. Send it round the far side of the block, under the surface, and get its fingers under the slab on my instep. A hand's all it is and a hand's all I need. Lift the slab toward you, away from me, and I'll pull the foot the second it eases."

While she works it, he does what he can from his side. His arm won't reach past the block — but his shortsword's two feet longer than his arm. He draws it slow under the water, turns it flat, and feeds the blade along his own shin, past the ankle, under the block's middle where the gap is half an inch, hunting for the slab's near edge with the point the way he'd hunt a lock's last pin with a pick. Lockpick's patience, not a labourer's shove: find the edge, set the point, then lever it a hair upward and outward with the guard braced against the block's underside.

"Bram — you're off the bar. Stay up. If that chock goes, I want you on the iron again before the block's down, not after. And somebody keep talking to me." He grinds the wrenched knee against the board on purpose, lets the pain cut through the sweet fog, and does *not* look at the gap behind the plaster, because he can feel it breathing on his knuckles and that's the sort of thing that can wait for daylight and a dry pair of boots.

To Hale, without turning his head: "Heavy-headed. Short shifts. And a case a season to a Gate house that stopped paying you the same week it bought this one." Flat. "I'll put that in my own words to Thorn. You'll want to be there."

[Roll the die]

[Onward]

The point finds the slab's edge like a pick finding its pin — a tiny catch, then a seat. Pell doesn't shove. He braces the guard against the block's underside, rolls his wrist a quarter-turn, and the crust lifts off his instep with a wet, grating sigh. The mud lets go of the boot a heartbeat later.

He pulls the leg the way he's been waiting to for half an hour: knee bent, foot pointed, straight back along the floor toward himself. It comes. All of it.

"*Clear.* Foot's out, Bram — let it down, easy, on your count, and get your own feet out from under it." He drags the shortsword back along his shin, slow, so it doesn't catch anything on the way, and sheathes it wet. Then he hauls hand over hand up the oak-anchored rope until he's clear of the block's fall-line, gets his good knee on the wedged board, and hangs there a moment with his forehead against the chalk wall, breathing daylight through his nose.

When the block's down and the water's done sloshing, he looks for Bram across it.

"You were meant to stay up." It's not a complaint. "Thank you. Now get out of this water before you start yawning too. Far wall, away from the broken lip — I'll be behind you on the line. The knee's not taking weight, so I'll be climbing on my arms; Second-Story Work says I can, and today it had better be right."

He gets a hand on the lifeline, tests it, and starts up the far wall — chimney-style, back and good foot and both hands, a yard at a time. Halfway, he pauses just long enough to hook two fingers under the silk rope where it still hangs from the prop, and tug once. The case swings and holds. Dry.

"Hale. When I'm up, you cut the box free and lower it on *this* line to whoever's below the hole — nobody leans. Then I want a strip of your apron for the knee and a straight piece of timber to lean on, and we'll both be at the Burning Wizard before Thorn is."

He doesn't look at the gap behind the plaster on the way past. He can still feel it breathing cold and sweet on his wet knuckles, and he's filing it where he files all the things that will still be there tomorrow.

Pell stops with the point of the sword against the packed gutter and thinks like a lockpick, not a miner: you don't dig a stuck pin out. You go round it.

"Bram — nothing of me is under that stone now. Let it down *on your count*, slow, onto the mud, and get your weight off the iron before your arms go. Then out of the water. I mean it — you've been breathing this as long as I have." He waits for the stone to be down before he moves again.

Then he sheathes the shortsword, reaches back into the pack still on his shoulders and comes out with a dagger. "Heel's set in a gutter like it's been mortared. I'm not digging that out blind. I'm cutting the boot." He feeds the dagger down along his shin, finds the top of the boot by touch, and starts opening it — down the inside seam from the cuff to the ankle, slow, point turned away from the skin, the way you'd slit a purse string without the owner feeling it. Laces, then leather. When the upper's open to the heel counter, he works his toes free, draws the foot up and out of the boot like a hand from a glove, and leaves the boot in the gutter for the quarry to keep.

"Hale, keep counting. Something else now — count me the seasons. How many cases of salt since you took the keys." The question's for himself as much as the man; a number to hold on to while his eyes want to close.

The moment the foot's clear he hauls on the oak rope, gets his good knee on the board, and goes for the far wall — back, foot and both arms, a yard at a time, head up out of the sweetness.
